conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is strabismus (squint)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Misalignment of the visual axes — the eyes point in different directions.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is amblyopia ('lazy eye')?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Reduced vision from abnormal visual development in childhood, in a structurally normal eye, because the developing brain suppresses the poorer image.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: How are strabismus and amblyopia linked?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Strabismus is a leading cause of amblyopia — the deviating eye's image is suppressed to avoid double vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Until roughly what age is the visual system plastic (the amblyopia treatment window)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Early childhood — treatment is most effective before about 7–8 years.It can still help older children, with lower response rates, so a late presentation is treated rather than abandoned.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is esotropia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: A convergent (inward-turning) squint — the commonest type in children.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is exotropia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: A divergent (outward-turning) squint.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is the difference between a tropia and a phoria?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back:
• A tropia is a manifest squint (present all the time)
  • a phoria is a latent squint (only appears when fusion is broken, e.g. on the cover test).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is the difference between concomitant and incomitant strabismus?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Concomitant: the angle is the SAME in all directions of gaze (commonest in children, usually refractive). Incomitant: the angle VARIES with gaze (paralytic/restrictive) — the more concerning type.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is accommodative esotropia and how is it treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back:
An esotropia driven by hypermetropia (the child over-accommodates to focus, turning the eye in).
  • In fully accommodative cases the full hypermetropic glasses correction straightens the eyes
  • in partially accommodative cases glasses reduce but do not abolish the squint, and the residual deviation may need surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is pseudostrabismus and how is it confirmed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Prominent epicanthic folds or a broad nasal bridge make the eyes look crossed although they are aligned; a symmetrical corneal light reflex and a normal cover test confirm it — reassure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: List the main causes of strabismus.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back:
• Refractive error (especially hypermetropia)
  • idiopathic/congenital
  • cranial nerve palsy (III/IV/VI)
  • sensory (reduced vision in one eye)
  • and neurological causes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What are the three types of amblyopia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back:
• Strabismic (suppression of a deviating eye)
  • refractive (anisometropic — unequal refractive error, or high bilateral error/astigmatism)
  • and stimulus deprivation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Which type of amblyopia is the most severe and most urgent to treat?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Stimulus-deprivation amblyopia (e.g. from congenital cataract, ptosis covering the pupil, or corneal opacity).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is the Hirschberg (corneal light reflex) test?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Shine a light at the eyes: the reflex is symmetrical and central when the eyes are aligned, and displaced in the deviating eye in a manifest squint.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What does the cover–uncover test detect?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: A manifest squint (tropia) — the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What does the alternate cover test detect?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: A latent squint (phoria).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: How is amblyopia defined?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Reduced best-corrected visual acuity in a structurally normal eye, with a known amblyogenic factor (strabismus, refractive error or deprivation).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Which sign in a child with a squint must prompt urgent referral, and how urgently?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back:
Leukocoria — an absent or abnormal red reflex — suggesting retinoblastoma or congenital cataract.
  • A new-onset squint TOGETHER WITH loss of the red reflex is an immediate referral (seen within hours)
  • an abnormal red reflex on its own is an urgent suspected-cancer referral, seen within 2 weeks (NICE).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: A childhood squint can be the presenting sign of which intraocular malignancy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Retinoblastoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Which features of a squint suggest a neurological cause?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: An incomitant (paralytic) squint, sudden onset, or a new squint in an older child — especially with headache or other neurology (think CN palsy, tumour, raised ICP).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Which investigation detects and quantifies hypermetropia in a squinting child?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Cycloplegic refraction.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is the first step in managing a child with a suspected squint or amblyopia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Refer to ophthalmology/orthoptics — immediately if a new squint comes with an absent red reflex, or with ataxia, vomiting or headache; urgently (within 2 weeks) for an abnormal red reflex on its own — and correct any refractive error with glasses.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: How is amblyopia treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: By penalising the GOOD eye to force use of the weaker eye — with occlusion (patching) or atropine penalisation — while the visual system is still plastic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Why is the GOOD eye (not the amblyopic eye) patched or blurred in amblyopia treatment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: To force the brain to use the weaker eye so its vision develops.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Where does squint surgery sit in the treatment order?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Usually after the refraction has been corrected and the amblyopia treated — for a residual, large or cosmetically significant deviation, or to restore binocular alignment.The exception is infantile (congenital) esotropia, where surgery is the primary treatment and is done early, aiming for alignment by about 2 years.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is the consequence of untreated amblyopia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Vision in the affected eye usually stays reduced into adulthood, with loss of stereopsis — amblyopia is the commonest cause of monocular visual impairment in children and young adults.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: Which refractive error typically underlies accommodative esotropia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.front: What is anisometropic amblyopia?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.back: Amblyopia caused by a difference in refractive error between the two eyes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular manifestations of diabetes mellitus?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back:
• Diabetic retinopathy/maculopathy
  • cataract
  • rubeosis iridis
  • and cranial nerve III (pupil-sparing) and VI palsies.
It is a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults, and the commonest preventable one.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular features of thyroid eye disease (Graves' orbitopathy)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back:
• Proptosis
  • lid retraction/lag
  • restrictive myopathy with diplopia
  • exposure keratopathy
  • and compressive optic neuropathy.
Smoking is the main modifiable risk factor — it makes the disease more likely, more severe and less responsive to treatment, so cessation is part of management; radioiodine can also trigger or worsen it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What is the sight-threatening complication of thyroid eye disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Compressive (dysthyroid) optic neuropathy — falling acuity, loss of colour vision and an RAPD.It needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, and orbital decompression if it does not respond quickly.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: Kayser–Fleischer rings are seen in which condition?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Wilson's disease — copper deposition at the corneal limbus (in a young person with liver and neuropsychiatric disease).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular features of vitamin A deficiency?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia and keratomalacia — a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness worldwide.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are Roth spots and what conditions cause them?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Retinal haemorrhages with pale centres — seen in infective endocarditis, leukaemia, anaemia and hyperviscosity states.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What ocular signs suggest infective endocarditis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Roth spots and conjunctival/splinter haemorrhages (with fever and a murmur).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: How does giant cell arteritis present in the eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Amaurosis fugax followed by sudden painless visual loss (arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, or central retinal artery occlusion).Raised ESR/CRP support it, but normal inflammatory markers do not exclude it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: An over-50 patient has sudden visual loss, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and a raised ESR. What is the diagnosis and immediate action?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Giant cell arteritis. Start steroids immediately to protect the fellow eye — intravenous methylprednisolone where there is visual loss, high-dose oral prednisolone where there is not.Then arrange temporal artery biopsy and/or ultrasound urgently; never delay steroids for the test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back:
• Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (secondary Sjögren's)
  • episcleritis
  • scleritis and peripheral ulcerative keratitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: How do scleritis and episcleritis differ clinically?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Scleritis causes severe, deep, boring pain that wakes the patient, with globe tenderness and a violaceous hue, and it threatens sight. Episcleritis is uncomfortable rather than truly painful and is self-limiting.At the bedside, episcleral vessels blanch with topical phenylephrine; scleral vessels do not.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: Which HLA type is associated with acute anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: HLA-B27 — seen in ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, IBD-associated and psoriatic arthritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular features of sarcoidosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back:
• Anterior and posterior uveitis
  • lacrimal gland enlargement and dry eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What ocular signs occur in GPA (granulomatosis with polyangiitis / Wegener's)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Scleritis, peripheral ulcerative keratitis and orbital granuloma causing proptosis (c-ANCA positive).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular features of Behçet's disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Recurrent uveitis and retinal vasculitis (with oral and genital ulcers).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: In whom does CMV retinitis occur and how does it look?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: In HIV/AIDS with a CD4 count below 50 — 'pizza-pie' retinal haemorrhages with exudate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What is an Argyll Robertson pupil and what causes it?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: A small, irregular pupil, usually bilateral, that accommodates but does not react to light — classically neurosyphilis (also diabetes).Size separates it from the large, tonic Holmes-Adie pupil, which also shows light-near dissociation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What is the commonest cause of posterior uveitis (chorioretinitis)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Toxoplasmosis — the commonest infectious cause, leaving a focal retinal scar (congenital or acquired).Non-infectious causes such as sarcoidosis are collectively common too.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the two classic ocular presentations of multiple sclerosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Optic neuritis and internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia that worsen at the end of the day suggest which condition?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Myasthenia gravis — ocular signs are often the first presentation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What is the ocular sign of raised intracranial pressure?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Papilloedema (bilateral optic disc swelling), often with a false-localising CN VI palsy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What is the triad of Horner's syndrome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis (± enophthalmos), from a lesion of the sympathetic pathway.Causes include Pancoast tumour, carotid dissection (painful, with neck pain — a red flag) and lateral medullary (Wallenberg) stroke. In a child think neuroblastoma; congenital Horner's may show heterochromia, the paler iris being the affected side.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: A patient has a painful CN III palsy with a fixed dilated pupil. What must be excluded?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm (a surgical, pupil-involving third nerve palsy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: In which direction does the lens dislocate in Marfan syndrome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Upwards (superotemporal) — ectopia lentis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: In which direction does the lens dislocate in homocystinuria?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Downwards (inferonasal) — ectopia lentis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are Lisch nodules and which condition are they associated with?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Iris hamartomas — neurofibromatosis type 1 (which also causes optic nerve glioma).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What ocular complication is associated with Sturge–Weber syndrome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Glaucoma, ipsilateral to the V1 port-wine stain.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What are the ocular findings in Down syndrome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Brushfield spots, cataract and keratoconus.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What ocular toxicity is caused by ethambutol?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: A dose-related optic neuropathy — reduced acuity, loss of red–green colour vision and a central scotoma.Check acuity and colour vision before starting, and warn the patient to stop the drug and report any visual change immediately; recovery depends on stopping early.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What retinal toxicity is caused by hydroxychloroquine?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Retinopathy — classically a bull's-eye maculopathy, but that is the late appearance.UK monitoring uses OCT and fundus autofluorescence annually from 5 years of treatment, earlier in higher-risk patients (dose above 5 mg/kg/day, renal impairment, concurrent tamoxifen). There is no routine baseline test for new starters (RCOphth).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: What corneal finding is caused by amiodarone?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Corneal verticillata (whorl-shaped deposits) — usually benign.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.front: Which drug can precipitate bilateral acute angle-closure glaucoma with a myopic shift?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.back: Topiramate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is the most common cause of infective conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Viral conjunctivitis, usually adenoviral — commonest overall and in adults. Age caveat: in young children a BACTERIAL cause is commoner, though most of those still settle without antibiotics.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: Name the three key discriminators that point to VIRAL conjunctivitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Watery (serous) discharge
  • a tender preauricular lymph node
  • and follicles on the everted tarsal conjunctiva
— usually with a recent URTI or sick contact.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: How does the discharge differ between viral, bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Viral: watery/serous
  • Bacterial: purulent and sticky (lids stuck on waking)
  • Allergic: watery/stringy mucoid

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What conjunctival reaction is characteristic of viral conjunctivitis, and how does it differ from bacterial/allergic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Follicles (small round pale lymphoid bumps) in viral; papillae in bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is the typical laterality of viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Often bilateral — starting in one eye and then involving the other.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: Which lymph node is characteristically tender/enlarged in viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: The preauricular node, just in front of the tragus. Tender and palpable in viral conjunctivitis and usually absent in ordinary bacterial and in allergic disease. The important exceptions are GONOCOCCAL and CHLAMYDIAL conjunctivitis, which also give a tender node — so a node with copious purulent discharge, or a chronic follicular picture in a sexually active adult, points away from adenovirus and towards urgent swabs and referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is pharyngoconjunctival fever (PCF)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: An adenoviral syndrome of fever + pharyngitis + follicular conjunctivitis, typically in children (adenovirus 3/4/7).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: A severe, highly contagious adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis (types 8/19/37) causing subepithelial corneal infiltrates → photophobia and blurred vision lasting weeks–months; occurs in outbreaks.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: Which viral cause of conjunctivitis is often unilateral with lid vesicles and a risk of a corneal dendritic ulcer?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Herpes simplex virus (HSV). Confirm with fluorescein, which shows a branching dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs; refer, and never start topical steroids empirically, because they can enlarge the ulcer and threaten sight.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: Why must topical steroids never be started empirically on a red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: If the cause is HSV, steroids can worsen a dendritic ulcer and threaten sight.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is Hutchinson's sign and what does it indicate?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: A vesicle on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus (nasociliary/V1 involvement) — it predicts ocular involvement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: How do itch and associated features differ between viral, bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Viral: grittiness or burning rather than true itch, often after a cold or sick contact
  • Bacterial: minimal itch, no systemic association
  • Allergic: prominent intense itch with atopy and rhinitis
Itch that DOMINATES the history points to allergy; grittiness after a cold points to adenovirus.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What should vision and the pupil look like in simple viral conjunctivitis, and what does a deviation mean?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Both normal. Reduced acuity, an abnormal pupil, severe pain, marked photophobia or ciliary flush means it is NOT simple conjunctivitis — think keratitis (including EKC), anterior uveitis or angle-closure, and refer the same day.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: List the red-eye red flags that mean it is NOT simple conjunctivitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Reduced visual acuity
  • severe pain
  • marked photophobia
  • ciliary (perilimbal) flush
  • a contact-lens wearer
  • or a neonate
— refer for same-day ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: A contact-lens wearer presents with a red eye. What must you assume until proven otherwise?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Microbial keratitis (e.g. Pseudomonas) — refer, do not treat as simple conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: In a neonate with conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which infections must be urgently excluded?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Gonococcal and chlamydial infection.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: Which bedside test excludes an HSV dendritic ulcer in a red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Fluorescein staining of the cornea.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What investigations are needed in viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Most cases need none — it is a clinical diagnosis. Fluorescein is the bedside test, to exclude an HSV dendritic ulcer and check for corneal involvement. Viral PCR/swab if severe, atypical, an outbreak (EKC) or occupationally needed; bacterial MC&S if bacterial is suspected, and urgently for suspected gonococcal/chlamydial infection.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is the natural course of viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Self-limiting — most settle within 1–3 weeks (EKC can take longer). It characteristically gets WORSE BEFORE BETTER: symptoms peak around 3–5 days and the second eye is often involved then. That worsening is expected and is not a reason to start antibiotics — new reduced vision, severe pain or marked photophobia is.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What supportive measures help viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Cool compresses
  • lubricants (artificial tears)
  • cleaning crusting with cooled boiled water or sterile saline
  • and simple analgesia
If ITCH dominates, reconsider the diagnosis — that is allergic conjunctivitis, which is where antihistamine drops belong.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is the role of topical antibiotics in viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: None. And not merely because the cause is viral: most acute infective conjunctivitis of any cause is self-limiting, and even where bacterial is likely a topical antibiotic shortens it by well under a day. Treat supportively and safety-net; refer rather than prescribe if gonococcal, chlamydial, neonatal, contact-lens-related or corneal involvement is suspected.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What are the complications of adenoviral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• EKC keratitis — subepithelial corneal infiltrates causing glare and blurred vision for weeks to months
  • secondary bacterial infection
  • and outbreaks, because it spreads readily through households, schools and eye clinics
Infection control remains the single most important management action.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What infection-control advice should be given?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back:
• Strict hand hygiene
  • avoid touching or rubbing the eyes
  • do not share towels, pillows or eye make-up
  • do not share eye drops
Exclusion from school, nursery or work is NOT routinely required — a child who is otherwise well can attend. Seek health-protection advice if there is an outbreak or cluster. Healthcare workers are the exception and should avoid direct patient contact while the eyes are red and watering. Take the patient to be infectious for roughly the first 10–14 days.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What should a contact-lens wearer with viral conjunctivitis be told about their lenses?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Stop lens wear until the eye is fully resolved, and discard the lenses and case. Separately, any contact-lens wearer whose red eye is painful or whose vision drops must be assumed to have microbial keratitis and referred — not managed as conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: When are topical steroids used in viral conjunctivitis and who should prescribe them?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Only for vision-threatening subepithelial infiltrates in EKC, and only under ophthalmology — after fluorescein has excluded a dendritic ulcer.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What is the main complication of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Subepithelial corneal infiltrates causing persistent glare and blurred vision for weeks to months.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.front: What safety-netting advice should patients with viral conjunctivitis receive?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.back: Return if vision becomes affected, pain becomes severe, marked photophobia develops, or it fails to settle — to reassess for keratitis or another cause.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Inflammation of the optic nerve — most often demyelinating — causing acute/subacute loss of vision in one eye, classically with pain on eye movement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the classic triad of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back:
• Subacute unilateral visual loss
  • pain on eye movement
  • impaired colour vision (dyschromatopsia / red desaturation)
Flashing lights (photopsia) may also occur, and the pain often precedes the visual loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the key examination sign of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) on the swinging-light test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Who typically gets optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Young to middle-aged adults, typically 20–50, women more than men; incidence peaks in the thirties. Onset in a child, or over 50, is atypical.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the most important association of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Multiple sclerosis — optic neuritis is often the first presenting demyelinating event.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is retrobulbar neuritis and how common is it?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Optic neuritis behind the globe, so the disc looks NORMAL (~2/3 of cases) — 'the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is papillitis (anterior optic neuritis)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Optic neuritis with a visibly SWOLLEN optic disc (~1/3 of cases; the other ~2/3 are retrobulbar with a normal disc). Unlike papilloedema it is usually unilateral, painful on eye movement, and reduces acuity and colour vision with a RAPD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Describe the colour-vision finding in optic neuritis and how it is tested.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Dyschromatopsia with red desaturation, often out of proportion to the acuity loss; tested with Ishihara plates.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is Uhthoff's phenomenon?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Transient worsening of vision with a rise in body temperature — heat or exercise.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What visual field defect is typical of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: A central scotoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the commonest type/cause of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Demyelinating optic neuritis — multiple sclerosis or a clinically isolated syndrome. The typical profile is a young adult, unilateral, painful on eye movement, with good spontaneous recovery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What antibody and clinical features characterise NMOSD-related optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies; it tends to be severe, often bilateral, with poor recovery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What antibody and features characterise MOGAD optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: MOG antibodies; often bilateral with disc swelling and very steroid-responsive.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: List atypical features of optic neuritis that should prompt a broader workup.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back:
• Bilateral involvement
  • no pain
  • no recovery or progressive loss
  • onset in a child or over 50
  • profound visual loss
  • marked disc swelling/haemorrhages
  • or systemic features
Progressive painless loss that never recovers also raises a COMPRESSIVE lesion — image it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Which toxic/nutritional causes mimic optic neuritis, and how do they differ?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Ethambutol, methanol and B12 deficiency cause optic neuropathy — but they are usually BILATERAL and PAINLESS (a mimic, not true neuritis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the key investigation in optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast (gadolinium).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What does MRI show in optic neuritis and why is it important?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: An enhancing/swollen optic nerve, and demyelinating white-matter lesions — the strongest predictor of future MS risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Which antibodies should be checked in atypical optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: AQP4 (NMOSD) and MOG (MOGAD) antibodies. Send them alongside the rest of the atypical panel: ESR/CRP, ACE for sarcoidosis, syphilis serology, B12 and an autoimmune screen — and consider Lyme and TB where the history fits.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What CSF finding supports an MS diagnosis on lumbar puncture?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Oligoclonal bands.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What do visual evoked potentials and OCT show in optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back:
• Visual evoked potentials show delayed latency with relatively preserved amplitude, useful in atypical or subclinical cases
  • OCT measures the retinal nerve fibre layer and is used for monitoring, showing later thinning as optic atrophy develops

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: How is typical demyelinating optic neuritis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: It is usually self-limiting and most patients recover without treatment, so steroid is NOT routine. High-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days, ± a short oral taper) is offered selectively — for severe or bilateral loss, or a functional need for faster recovery. Refer urgently to ophthalmology, and to neurology for the MS workup and disease-modifying therapy if MS is confirmed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the effect of high-dose IV methylprednisolone on visual recovery and on the final visual outcome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: It SPEEDS visual recovery but does NOT change the final visual outcome — which is why it is used selectively rather than routinely.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Why should standard-dose oral prednisolone alone be avoided in optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Standard-dose oral prednisolone on its own does not speed recovery and INCREASES the recurrence rate of optic neuritis. The steroid must be high dose, or not given at all — it is the dose that matters.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: When is treatment with IV steroids particularly considered in optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back:
• Severe or bilateral visual loss
  • or a functional/occupational need (e.g. an only-seeing eye)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the visual recovery like in demyelinating optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Vision usually begins to improve at 2–4 weeks and most patients recover good acuity over weeks to months.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What residual deficits can persist after optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back:
• Reduced colour and contrast sensitivity
  • persistent Uhthoff's phenomenon
  • and later optic atrophy (a pale disc)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: What is the risk of developing MS after a single episode of optic neuritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: Roughly 50% develop MS by 15 years, but MRI splits that sharply: with one or more demyelinating lesions the risk is about three in four, with a normal scan about one in four.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.front: Why is it important to identify NMOSD rather than treat all optic neuritis as MS?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.back: NMOSD has a worse visual prognosis and is managed differently (e.g. plasma exchange and longer-term immunosuppression), so it must not be treated as simple MS.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is periorbital (preseptal) cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Infection of the soft tissues ANTERIOR to the orbital septum — confined to the eyelid and periorbital skin.The globe and orbit are not involved. It is common and usually benign.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is orbital (postseptal) cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Infection POSTERIOR to the orbital septum, within the orbit itself (fat, extraocular muscles, around the optic nerve).It is a sight- and life-threatening emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What structure separates preseptal from orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: The orbital septum — a thin fibrous sheet running from the periosteum of the orbital rim to the tarsal plates of the eyelids.It acts as the barrier that contains infection.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which antibiotics treat preseptal cellulitis, including if the patient is penicillin-allergic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: First line is oral co-amoxiclav. If penicillin-allergic: clindamycin, or clarithromycin PLUS metronidazole in adults (clarithromycin alone may suffice in children).Orbital cellulitis instead needs IV antibiotics.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What clinical feature do BOTH preseptal and orbital cellulitis share?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: A unilateral red, swollen, warm, tender eyelid.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Name the key red flags that indicate ORBITAL (postseptal) cellulitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Proptosis
  • painful and restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia) with diplopia
  • reduced visual acuity or colour vision / a RAPD
  • chemosis
  • and systemic toxicity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: How do you assess for proptosis at the bedside in a swollen eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Look from above and behind the patient, over the brow, comparing the corneal positions
  • measure with exophthalmometry
  • and test retropulsion — resistance to gentle retropulsion of the globe suggests postseptal involvement.
Proptosis is absent in preseptal cellulitis and is the hallmark of orbital cellulitis, though it can be absent early or hidden by a tense swollen lid.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: How do eye movements differ between preseptal and orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Preseptal: full and painless. Orbital: painful and restricted (ophthalmoplegia), often with diplopia.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What happens to visual acuity and colour vision in orbital vs preseptal cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Preseptal: normal. Orbital: reduced acuity and colour vision from optic nerve involvement — a red flag.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which test detects the EARLIEST sign of optic nerve compromise in orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Colour vision (Ishihara plates) — red desaturation is an early marker; also check for a RAPD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is the single most common cause of orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Direct spread from paranasal sinusitis — especially ETHMOID sinusitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Why does ethmoid sinusitis so readily cause orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: The ethmoid air cells are separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea, so infection tracks straight through.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: In which age group is orbital cellulitis most common, and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Children — because it follows ethmoid sinusitis, which is common in childhood, and because the lamina papyracea is thin and often dehiscent, the orbit and sinuses share valveless veins, and immunity is relatively immature.Incidence peaks in winter alongside sinusitis.It is sight- and life-threatening at ANY age, including in adults.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: List common causes of PRESEPTAL cellulitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: A local skin breach — insect bite, trauma/laceration — or spread from an adjacent infection (stye/hordeolum, chalazion, dacryocystitis, conjunctivitis, impetigo); URTI/sinusitis in children.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which organisms typically cause peri-/orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Staphylococcus aureus (consider MRSA)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Strep pyogenes (Group A)
  • and non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (Hib now rare post-vaccine).
Anaerobes/polymicrobial in older children and adults.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which fungal infection must you consider in a diabetic (DKA) or immunocompromised patient with orbital cellulitis, and how is it treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Mucormycosis (or invasive Aspergillus) — look for a black necrotic eschar on the palate/nasal mucosa. Treat with urgent biopsy, systemic antifungals (liposomal amphotericin B) and aggressive surgical debridement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is the Chandler classification of orbital infection?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• I: preseptal cellulitis
  • II: orbital cellulitis
  • III: subperiosteal abscess
  • IV: orbital abscess
  • V: cavernous sinus thrombosis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is the key imaging investigation in suspected orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, paranasal sinuses and brain.MRI is reserved for suspected cavernous sinus thrombosis or intracranial spread.Lumbar puncture is done only if there is meningism, and only AFTER imaging.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What does the CT tell you in orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Confirms post-septal (orbital) involvement
  • identifies a subperiosteal or orbital abscess
  • shows the sinus source
  • and detects intracranial extension.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which laboratory tests are done in peri-/orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• FBC (neutrophilia)
  • CRP/ESR (raised — monitor response)
  • and blood cultures before antibiotics — taken with the first cannula, and never allowed to delay them.
Also swab any eye or wound discharge, plus a nasal swab, to guide antibiotic choice.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: How is PRESEPTAL cellulitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Oral co-amoxiclav — or, if penicillin-allergic, clindamycin, or clarithromycin PLUS metronidazole in adults. Analgesia, review at 24–48 h in eye casualty or by ophthalmology, and explicit safety-netting for the orbital red flags.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: When should preseptal cellulitis be admitted for IV treatment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• If the child is under 1 year
  • systemically unwell
  • not improving/worsening on oral antibiotics
  • or orbital involvement cannot be excluded.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Outline the management of ORBITAL cellulitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Admit
  • urgent joint ophthalmology + ENT review
  • IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, per local policy — typically ceftriaxone + flucloxacillin + metronidazole, swapping flucloxacillin for vancomycin or teicoplanin only if there is a specific MRSA risk
  • CT orbits/sinuses/brain
  • treat the sinusitis
  • monitor visual function hourly
  • surgical drainage if indicated.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What are the indications for surgery in orbital cellulitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• An abscess on CT
  • no improvement or deterioration at 24–48 h despite IV antibiotics
  • or any decline in visual function.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: What is orbital compartment syndrome and how is it treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: A tense, proptosed eye with rising orbital pressure and falling vision (± RAPD). It needs emergency lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis to decompress the orbit and save the optic nerve — do not wait for imaging.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Which life-threatening intracranial complication should you suspect when orbital signs become BILATERAL?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — bilateral eye signs with cranial nerve palsies (III, IV, V1/V2, VI), severe headache and rapid deterioration.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: List the major complications of orbital cellulitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back:
• Subperiosteal/orbital abscess
  • vision loss (optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, orbital compartment syndrome)
  • intracranial spread (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess)
  • sepsis and death.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.front: Why must you examine the globe even when the eyelid is swollen shut?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Periorbital &.back: To detect orbital involvement (eye movements, pupil/RAPD, acuity) — you cannot exclude orbital cellulitis without assessing the eye, and this is especially important in children.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is uveitis and which is the commonest form?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Inflammation of the uveal tract (the pigmented middle layer — iris, ciliary body, choroid). Anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis — inflammation of the iris ± ciliary body) is the commonest form (~75%).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Why does anterior uveitis matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: It is a leading cause of the painful red eye with photophobia, the classic HLA-B27/seronegative spondyloarthropathy eye disease (a major rheumatology crossover), it recurs, and untreated it causes sight-threatening complications (posterior synechiae, glaucoma, cataract, macular oedema).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What makes up the uvea, and how is uveitis classified by site?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
The uvea = iris + ciliary body + choroid. Classified as
  • anterior (iris/ciliary body)
  • intermediate (vitreous)
  • posterior (choroid/retina)
  • or panuveitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the pathophysiology of the signs in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Inflammation of the anterior chamber causes breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier, so white cells and protein leak into the anterior chamber — producing the hallmark 'cells and flare'.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How do anterior and posterior uveitis differ in presentation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Anterior (iris ± ciliary body): painful, red, photophobic; signs = anterior chamber cells/flare, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae
  • Posterior (choroid/retina): often painless, white eye; main symptoms = floaters and visual loss; signs = vitritis and chorioretinal lesions.
Posterior disease should always prompt a search for an infective cause (toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis in the immunosuppressed, TB, syphilis) or systemic disease (sarcoidosis, Behçet's), and needs dilated fundoscopy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How does acute differ from chronic anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Acute: sudden, painful, self-limiting, recurrent (classic HLA-B27 pattern)
  • Chronic: insidious, less painful (e.g. JIA, sarcoidosis) — more dangerous because it is quiet.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the clinical symptoms of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• A painful red eye (a dull ache over hours–days, usually unilateral)
  • often severe photophobia (ciliary muscle spasm) with pain worse on accommodation or near work
  • excessive watering
  • and blurred vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is consensual photophobia and why is it useful?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Shining light in the OTHER (unaffected) eye causes pain in the affected eye. It means true intraocular or corneal inflammation, so it separates anterior uveitis from conjunctivitis — but it also occurs in keratitis and corneal abrasion, so it does not mean 'uveitis' on its own.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is ciliary flush?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Circumcorneal injection — redness concentrated around the limbus/cornea (vs the diffuse, fornix-based redness of conjunctivitis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the pupil like in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Small (miosis from iris spasm) and may be irregular if posterior synechiae have formed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the defining slit-lamp sign of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Anterior chamber 'cells and flare' — inflammatory cells plus protein producing a hazy/'milky' beam.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are keratic precipitates (KPs)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Clumps of inflammatory cells deposited on the corneal endothelium — a slit-lamp sign of uveitis. Large 'mutton-fat' KPs suggest granulomatous causes (e.g. sarcoidosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is a hypopyon and which causes are classic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A layer of white cells in the anterior chamber — classic in HLA-B27-associated uveitis and Behçet's disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are posterior synechiae and their danger?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Adhesions where the iris sticks to the lens → an irregular/festooned pupil → risk of iris bombé → glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Roughly what proportion of anterior uveitis has a systemic association?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: About 50%.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the HLA-B27-associated causes of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Ankylosing spondylitis (commonest — young man, inflammatory back pain)
  • reactive arthritis ('can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree')
  • psoriatic arthritis
  • and inflammatory bowel disease (UC/Crohn's).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What non-HLA-B27 systemic conditions are associated with uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Sarcoidosis (granulomatous — 'mutton-fat' KPs)
  • Behçet's (uveitis + hypopyon + oral/genital ulcers)
  • juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA — chronic and painless; all children with JIA need slit-lamp screening, highest risk ANA-positive oligoarticular)
  • multiple sclerosis (intermediate)
  • and infective causes (HSV/VZV, TB, syphilis, toxoplasmosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: Why is JIA-associated uveitis particularly dangerous, and who is screened?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Because it is chronic and painless ('white' uveitis) — the eye is neither red nor sore — so it goes unnoticed until sight-threatening complications (cataract, glaucoma, band keratopathy) have developed. Every child with JIA is therefore slit-lamp screened regardless of symptoms; ANA-positive oligoarticular children are the highest-risk group and are screened most often.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the classic exam stem for HLA-B27 anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A young man with a painful, photophobic red eye + hypopyon + inflammatory back pain → HLA-B27 anterior uveitis with ankylosing spondylitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the key investigation in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Slit-lamp examination (cells/flare, KPs, hypopyon, synechiae)
  • dilated fundoscopy for posterior involvement
  • and measuring IOP (uveitic glaucoma).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: When is a systemic work-up needed in anterior uveitis, and what does it include?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: A first typical mild episode often needs none. Recurrent, bilateral, granulomatous, or with systemic features → investigate: HLA-B27, FBC/ESR/CRP, ACE + CXR (sarcoid), syphilis serology, TB (IGRA/CXR), ANA (JIA in children), and imaging for spondyloarthropathy — guided by history.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How urgently should suspected acute anterior uveitis be seen, and what is the first-line treatment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Same-day ophthalmology assessment — the diagnosis needs a slit lamp. First-line treatment is a topical corticosteroid (prednisolone acetate 1%, frequent dosing then tapered) to suppress the inflammation, started by ophthalmology after slit-lamp diagnosis — never on an undiagnosed red eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is the role of a cycloplegic/mydriatic in anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Cyclopentolate/atropine dilate the pupil to relieve pain (paralysing ciliary spasm) and to prevent/break posterior synechiae (keeping the iris moving off the lens).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What treatments are used for severe/posterior/resistant or chronic uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Periocular or systemic steroids for severe/posterior/resistant disease
  • and systemic immunosuppression/biologics (methotrexate, anti-TNF such as adalimumab) for chronic, recurrent or sight-threatening uveitis (with rheumatology).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: How is infective uveitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Treat the underlying cause with antimicrobials — e.g. aciclovir for herpetic uveitis — and manage any associated systemic disease. Monitor and treat uveitic glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What are the complications of anterior uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back:
• Posterior synechiae → irregular pupil, iris bombé → acute glaucoma
  • cataract (inflammation + steroid use)
  • glaucoma (uveitic or steroid-induced)
  • cystoid macular oedema (a common cause of visual loss)
  • band keratopathy (chronic — calcium in the cornea)
  • and vision loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.front: What is a common cause of visual loss in uveitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Uveitis / Iri.back: Cystoid macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Inflammation of the outer coats of the eye — episcleritis affects the episclera (thin vascular layer between conjunctiva and sclera), and scleritis affects the sclera (tough white outer wall).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How do episcleritis and scleritis differ in seriousness?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis is a benign, self-limiting nuisance
  • scleritis is a painful, sight-threatening emergency strongly linked to systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease and can be the first sign of life-threatening granulomatosis with polyangiitis

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the core clinical distinction between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis = superficial, mild, mobile vessels that blanch, minimal/no pain, self-limiting
  • Scleritis = deep, severe boring pain, immobile violaceous vessels that don't blanch, systemic disease, refer urgently

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the phenylephrine (blanching) test and its results?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Instil one drop of phenylephrine 2.5% and re-examine after about 10 minutes: episcleral (superficial) vessels blanch and the eye whitens (episcleritis); scleral (deep) vessels persist and do NOT blanch (scleritis). It is the key discriminator. The low 2.5% strength is used — 10% is avoided for its systemic pressor effect.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the pain of episcleritis compare with scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis: mild/no pain (gritty discomfort)
  • Scleritis: severe, deep, boring pain — worse at night (wakes from sleep), worse on eye movement

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the redness differ between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis: bright red/salmon-pink, sectoral
  • Scleritis: deep violaceous/bluish-red

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the tenderness and vessel mobility difference between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis: not tender; superficial vessels are mobile with a cotton bud
  • Scleritis: globe tender to touch; deep vessels are immobile

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Does vision differ between episcleritis and scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis: vision normal
  • Scleritis: vision may be reduced

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the systemic associations of episcleritis vs scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Episcleritis: usually idiopathic
  • Scleritis: ~50% have systemic autoimmune/vasculitic disease

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the clinical features of episcleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Acute red eye, usually sectoral (a wedge, sometimes diffuse); mild/no pain (discomfort, watering, gritty); no visual impairment, no discharge, minimal/no photophobia. Simple (diffuse/sectoral) or nodular (a mobile nodule) forms; mostly idiopathic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How is episcleritis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
Self-limiting —
  • reassurance often all that's needed (~1–2 weeks)
  • lubricants for comfort
  • topical/oral NSAIDs if troublesome
  • topical steroids occasionally (specialist)
Investigate only if recurrent/atypical. But if the blanching is equivocal, the pain is more than mild, the globe is tender or vision is reduced, treat it as scleritis and refer the same day.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the features of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Severe, deep, 'boring' ocular pain radiating to brow/jaw/temple, worse at night and on eye movement (extraocular muscles insert into the sclera)
  • globe tenderness
  • deep violaceous injection
  • may have reduced vision, photophobia, watering
  • often bilateral and recurrent
  • can involve the cornea/uvea

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Why is scleritis pain worse on eye movement?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Because the extraocular muscles insert into the sclera.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What are the subtypes of ANTERIOR scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Diffuse (best prognosis)
  • nodular (an immobile tender nodule)
  • necrotising WITH inflammation (most severe — scleral destruction, strong vasculitis association, high morbidity/mortality)
  • and necrotising WITHOUT inflammation (scleromalacia perforans — painless scleral thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is scleromalacia perforans?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Necrotising scleritis without inflammation — painless scleral thinning in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is necrotising scleritis with inflammation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: The most severe form — scleral destruction with a strong vasculitis association and high morbidity/mortality.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is posterior scleritis and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Scleritis behind the equator, causing proptosis, pain on movement, disc swelling and retinal/choroidal changes. Harder to diagnose — needs B-scan ultrasound (the 'T-sign').

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the commonest systemic association of scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Rheumatoid arthritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: Which vasculitis can present with scleritis and must not be missed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA/Wegener's) and other ANCA-associated vasculitides — scleritis may be the presenting feature of life-threatening vasculitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: List the systemic associations of scleritis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
• Rheumatoid arthritis (commonest)
  • GPA/Wegener's and other ANCA-associated vasculitides
  • SLE
  • relapsing polychondritis
  • IBD
  • sarcoidosis
  • and infective causes (herpes zoster, TB, syphilis; gout)
Seronegative spondyloarthropathy is a much weaker association here — HLA-B27 disease is the classic cause of anterior uveitis, not scleritis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What systemic work-up is done in scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
With rheumatology:
  • FBC
  • ESR/CRP
  • U&Es + urinalysis (renal vasculitis)
  • ANCA (GPA)
  • RF/anti-CCP
  • ANA/anti-dsDNA
  • ACE (sarcoid)
  • infection screen (syphilis, TB, HSV/VZV)
  • B-scan for posterior scleritis (T-sign)
  • CXR (sarcoid/GPA/TB)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the management ladder for scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back:
Same-day ophthalmology referral plus a systemic work-up. Then:
  • (1) a systemic NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose — first-line for non-necrotising scleritis
  • (2) a systemic corticosteroid (oral, or IV pulsed if severe) if that fails
  • (3) steroid-sparing immunosuppression or biologics under rheumatology for necrotising or vasculitic disease (methotrexate, mycophenolate; cyclophosphamide or rituximab in ANCA-associated vasculitis)
Treat any underlying systemic or infective cause. Topical steroids are adjunctive only — never the whole treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for non-necrotising scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: A full anti-inflammatory dose of an oral NSAID — ibuprofen or naproxen (flurbiprofen or indomethacin are alternatives) — with gastroprotection considered.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.front: How does the nodule of nodular episcleritis differ from that of nodular scleritis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Scleritis / E.back: The episcleritis nodule is MOBILE; the scleritis nodule is IMMOBILE.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Separation of the neurosensory retina (photoreceptors) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) — the light-sensing layer lifts off the tissue that nourishes it. It is a time-critical, sight-threatening emergency: the detached retina loses its blood/nutrient supply and photoreceptors die within days.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What holds the neurosensory retina and RPE together, and what happens if fluid gets between them?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: They are only loosely apposed, held together by vitreous pressure and RPE pumping. If fluid gets between them (through a tear, from traction, or by exudation), the retina detaches and photoreceptors lose RPE support and degenerate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are the three types of retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
• Rhegmatogenous (commonest — a retinal break/tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retina)
  • tractional (fibrous tissue pulls the retina off)
  • and exudative/serous (fluid leaks under the retina with no break or traction)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
A retinal break/tear lets vitreous fluid pass under the retina — associated with
  • posterior vitreous detachment (PVD)
  • myopia
  • trauma
  • previous cataract surgery
  • and lattice degeneration

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes tractional retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
Fibrous tissue pulling the retina off — e.g.
  • proliferative diabetic retinopathy
  • sickle cell disease
  • and prior trauma

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What causes exudative (serous) retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
Fluid leaking under the retina with no break and no traction — from
  • inflammation
  • tumour
  • malignant hypertension/pre-eclampsia
  • or central serous retinopathy

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What does 'rhegmatogenous' mean, and why is it important?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: From 'rhegma' (a break) — it is the classic and commonest type, presenting with flashes/floaters/curtain and needing urgent surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the biggest risk factor for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Myopia (short-sightedness) — a longer, thinner eye/retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the key precipitant of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) — the ageing vitreous pulls on the retina and can cause a tear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: List the risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
• Myopia (biggest)
  • posterior vitreous detachment (key precipitant)
  • increasing age (50s–70s)
  • previous cataract surgery (pseudophakia)
  • ocular trauma
  • previous retinal detachment (or in the other eye)
  • family history
  • lattice degeneration
  • and diabetic retinopathy (tractional type)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the warning triad of retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
• Flashes (photopsia)
  • floaters (a sudden increase or shower)
  • and a 'curtain'/'shadow' spreading across the visual field — which may come down from above or rise from below, as it appears opposite the detached retina
All painless.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are flashes (photopsia) in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Brief peripheral flashes of light caused by vitreous traction on the retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What do different floaters suggest in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
• A sudden increase/shower of black spots or a 'cobweb'
  • a large single floater (Weiss ring) suggests PVD
  • a shower of tiny dots ('tobacco dust'/Shafer's sign) suggests a retinal tear

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the 'curtain' or 'shadow' in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: A progressive, painless shadow or curtain spreading across the visual field. It appears opposite the detached retina — a superior detachment gives a shadow rising from below, an inferior detachment a curtain coming down — and it advances towards the centre as the detachment extends, reaching the centre when the macula detaches.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What happens to central vision in retinal detachment, and what sign appears in large detachments?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Central vision is preserved until the macula detaches; once the macula goes, central acuity drops and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) may appear in large detachments.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How is posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) distinguished from retinal detachment clinically?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: PVD alone (very common, benign) also causes flashes and floaters — but a curtain/shadow or reduced vision suggests the PVD has caused a tear/detachment → refer. Any new flashes/floaters need assessment to exclude a break.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the significance of 'macula-ON' retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: The macula is still attached and central vision is intact → EXTREMELY urgent: operate before the macula detaches to preserve central vision (best outcomes, ideally within ~24 h). While waiting, posture the patient to keep fluid away from the macula.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the significance of 'macula-OFF' retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: The macula has already detached and central vision is lost. The referral is still same-day; it is the surgical window that is slightly less frantic (ideally within ~2–3 days). Visual prognosis is already compromised, as central vision often does not fully recover. Macula status is determined by the ophthalmologist on dilated examination — it never downgrades the urgency of the referral itself.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the key diagnostic test in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Dilated fundus examination (indirect ophthalmoscopy) — shows the detached retina (grey, elevated, mobile), identifies breaks/tears, and whether the macula is on or off.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is Shafer's sign?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Pigment cells/'tobacco dust' in the anterior vitreous on slit-lamp — suggestive of a retinal tear.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: When is B-scan ultrasound used in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: If the view is obscured (e.g. by vitreous haemorrhage or cataract).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the role of OCT in retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: It confirms whether the macula is on or off when the clinical view is equivocal — which determines the surgical urgency. At the bedside you record visual acuity in both eyes and check for an RAPD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the initial management of any suspected retinal detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Refer for same-day ophthalmology assessment. While awaiting surgery, posture the patient to keep subretinal fluid away from the macula (position depends on the break location) and avoid strenuous activity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How is a retinal TEAR (before detachment) treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back: Laser retinopexy or cryotherapy — seals the break to prevent (further) detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What are the surgical options for established rhegmatogenous detachment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
• Pars plana vitrectomy (removes vitreous, drains subretinal fluid, seals breaks, plus gas or silicone oil tamponade) — the usual choice for most modern detachments
  • scleral buckling (a silicone band indents the sclera, favoured in younger phakic eyes and in retinal dialysis after blunt trauma)
  • and pneumatic retinopexy for a selected superior break
While a gas bubble remains the patient must posture as instructed and must not fly, travel to altitude, or have nitrous oxide anaesthesia — the bubble expands and can raise intraocular pressure enough to cause permanent visual loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: How are tractional and exudative retinal detachments managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
Treat the underlying cause —
  • laser/vitrectomy for diabetic tractional detachment
  • BP control or treatment of tumour/inflammation for exudative detachment

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.front: What is the golden rule for new flashes and floaters?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Retinal Detac.back:
Exclude a retinal tear. PVD alone is benign, but a curtain/shadow or reduced vision means same-day emergency referral. Even without those, new flashes or floaters need a dilated fundus examination within 24 hours to exclude a break — then reassure and safety-net: return immediately if
  • the floaters shower
  • the flashes worsen
  • a curtain appears
  • or vision drops

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Retinal damage from chronic (or acutely severe) high blood pressure — the eye's version of hypertensive target-organ damage.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Why does hypertensive retinopathy matter clinically?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
• The retina is the only place you can directly see the effects of hypertension on blood vessels
  • the grade correlates with cardiovascular/stroke risk and mortality
  • and its most severe form (grade 4/papilloedema) signals malignant (accelerated) hypertension — a medical emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are the three phases of hypertensive retinopathy pathophysiology?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
• (1) Vasoconstrictive — arterioles constrict → generalised narrowing
  • (2) sclerotic — chronic pressure thickens the walls (arteriosclerosis) → copper/silver wiring + AV nipping
  • (3) exudative — the blood-retinal barrier breaks down → haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and (if severe) optic disc swelling.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the key fork in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Chronic hypertensive change with no acute features — sustained high BP, manage BP and cardiovascular risk — versus accelerated/malignant hypertension: clinic BP 180/120 or higher with retinal haemorrhage OR papilloedema, which needs same-day specialist assessment (NICE). Note the emergency trigger is haemorrhage or papilloedema, not papilloedema alone, so a grade 3 fundus at that pressure is also an emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What grading system is used for hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification (grades 1–4), where each grade builds on the previous.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 1 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Mild generalised arteriolar narrowing (vessels look thinner), ± increased tortuosity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 1 + focal arteriolar narrowing + AV nipping/nicking. (Copper wiring reflects moderate arteriolar sclerosis and is often described here, but sources differ on which grade it belongs to, so do not use it to assign a grade.)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 2 + flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates. (Silver wiring reflects severe arteriolar sclerosis and is often described here, but sources differ on which grade it belongs to.)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What defines Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Grade 3 + papilloedema ± macular star = malignant hypertension.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is AV nipping (nicking)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: The vein appears pinched or deviated where a thickened, sclerotic artery crosses it — a sign of arteriosclerosis in hypertensive retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the difference between copper wiring and silver wiring?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
Increasingly sclerotic arterioles reflect light abnormally:
  • copper wiring = moderate sclerosis
  • silver wiring = severe sclerosis.
They mark the severity of arteriolosclerosis rather than defining a specific grade — sources differ on which grade each belongs to.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are cotton-wool spots and what do they represent?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Fluffy white patches that are nerve-fibre-layer microinfarcts (ischaemia).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are flame haemorrhages?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Superficial nerve-fibre-layer bleeds seen in hypertensive retinopathy (grade 3).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is a macular star?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Hard exudates (lipid/protein leakage) arranged in a star pattern around the fovea — seen in severe hypertensive retinopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What does papilloedema indicate in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Optic disc swelling (grade 4) = malignant hypertension — a medical emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Is hypertensive retinopathy usually symptomatic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Usually asymptomatic — found on routine fundoscopy. Malignant hypertension may cause headache, visual disturbance/blurring, and features of other end-organ damage (AKI, heart failure, encephalopathy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What does sudden visual loss in a patient with hypertensive retinopathy suggest?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: A complication such as a retinal vein or artery occlusion (hypertension is a major risk factor).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What investigations are used in hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
Blood pressure + fundoscopy/dilated fundus exam (grade the changes) drive the diagnosis. Assess other target-organ damage:
  • urinalysis + U&Es (renal)
  • ECG/echo (LVH)
  • fundus photography/OCT/FFA for documentation.
Screen for secondary hypertension if young/severe/resistant.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What is the mainstay of treatment for hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Controlling the blood pressure — it is not primarily an 'eye' treatment. Most retinal changes stabilise or improve with good BP control.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How is chronic (grades 1–3) hypertensive retinopathy managed?
