conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Manage hypertension per standard guidelines (lifestyle + antihypertensives — ACE inhibitor/ARB, calcium-channel blocker, thiazide-like diuretic, per NICE) and address global cardiovascular risk (lipids, diabetes, smoking cessation).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How is accelerated/malignant hypertension managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Same-day specialist assessment or admission for clinic BP 180/120 or higher with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or acute end-organ damage (NICE). Lower BP GRADUALLY — never crash it. If retinopathy is the only acute finding, use ORAL therapy, reducing BP over 24–48 hours and then progressively over the following weeks with close review. IV agents such as labetalol are reserved for a true hypertensive emergency — encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute LVF, eclampsia — where MAP is reduced by no more than about 25% in the first hour.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: Why must blood pressure be lowered GRADUALLY in malignant hypertension?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back: Because rapid reduction risks watershed cerebral, retinal and renal ischaemia and infarction — the brain and kidney have shifted their autoregulation upwards. If retinopathy is the only acute finding, treat orally and gradually over 24–48 hours and then over the following weeks. Where IV therapy is genuinely indicated, reduce MAP by no more than about 25% in the first hour.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: What are the complications of hypertensive retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
• Retinal vein or artery occlusion (hypertension is a major risk factor)
  • macular oedema/exudative retinal detachment (severe cases)
  • optic atrophy (prolonged papilloedema) → permanent visual loss
  • and worsening of co-existing diabetic retinopathy
it also marks elevated stroke/cardiac/renal risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.front: How do hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy signs differ on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Hypertensive.back:
• Hypertension: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper/silver wiring.
  • Diabetes: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, neovascularisation.
(Cotton-wool spots occur in both.)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is herpes simplex keratitis and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Corneal infection/inflammation caused by herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) — the commonest infective cause of corneal blindness in the developed world. It is a sight-threatening cause of the painful red eye, it recurs, and topical steroids given for the epithelial form can dramatically worsen it and cause corneal perforation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the single most important teaching point about HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical corticosteroids given for the epithelial (dendritic) form dramatically worsen it and can cause corneal perforation — it is the classic reason NEVER to give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the mechanism of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: After primary infection, HSV-1 lies latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Triggers cause reactivation → the virus travels down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) to the cornea → replicates in the epithelium → the characteristic branching dendritic ulcer. Repeated episodes drive stromal scarring and vision loss.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: Where does HSV-1 lie latent, and which nerve division does it travel down to reach the cornea?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Latent in the trigeminal ganglion; it reactivates and travels down the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the key fork in HSV keratitis, and what does it determine?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Epithelial (dendritic) vs stromal/disciform disease — this determines whether steroids are dangerous or necessary (the crux of management).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the nature and treatment of EPITHELIAL (dendritic) HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Active viral replication in the epithelium; the sign is a dendritic ulcer (branching, stains with fluorescein). Treatment is a topical antiviral with same-day ophthalmology assessment; topical steroids are CONTRAINDICATED, and the eye must never be padded or patched.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the nature and treatment of STROMAL/disciform HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Immune-mediated stromal inflammation; signs include stromal haze/oedema, a disciform disc of oedema, neovascularisation and scarring. Treatment is antiviral PLUS topical steroid (under specialist supervision).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the 'golden rule' about steroids in epithelial HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: In epithelial (dendritic) disease, topical steroids promote viral replication → the dendrite enlarges into a geographic ('amoeboid') ulcer → risk of perforation. Steroids are only used in stromal/disciform (immune-driven) disease, always with antiviral cover under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: List the risk factors/triggers for HSV keratitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back:
• Previous HSV eye disease (recurrence is the rule)
  • UV/sunlight exposure
  • fever/systemic illness
  • physical/emotional stress
  • menstruation
  • immunosuppression (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy)
  • atopic disease
  • topical/systemic corticosteroids
  • contact lens wear
  • and ocular surgery

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What are the clinical features of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back:
• A painful, red, unilateral eye with foreign-body/gritty sensation, watering, photophobia
  • blurred vision if the central cornea/stroma is involved
  • reduced corneal sensation (a useful clue)
  • and possibly vesicles on the eyelids/periocular skin

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: Why is reduced corneal sensation a useful clue in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Because HSV damages the corneal nerves, reducing corneal sensation — a helpful diagnostic pointer.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the pathognomonic sign of epithelial HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: A dendritic ulcer — a branching, serpentine epithelial ulcer with terminal bulbs that stains with fluorescein (green under blue light). (Specialists may also use Rose Bengal, which stains devitalised cells at the ulcer edges — fluorescein is the one to know.)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the key first investigation in suspected HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein — usually diagnostic (a dendrite confirms it) and assesses for stromal involvement.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What additional tests may be used in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Corneal sensation testing (reduced in HSV) and viral swab/PCR (corneal/conjunctival) if uncertain or atypical.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What must you NOT do before slit-lamp + fluorescein in any painful red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Do NOT start steroid drops — fluorescein must first exclude a dendritic ulcer (steroids would risk a geographic ulcer/perforation).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the topical antiviral treatment for epithelial (dendritic) HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical antiviral — ganciclovir 0.15% eye gel or aciclovir 3% eye ointment, 5×/day until the ulcer heals, then tapered. Started the same day, under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: When are oral antivirals used in HSV keratitis, and what other measures help epithelial disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: An oral antiviral (aciclovir/valaciclovir) in some cases, and in immunocompromised, severe or recurrent disease. Epithelial debridement (specialist) and a cycloplegic (cyclopentolate) for comfort also help — a cycloplegic is safe here, unlike in acute angle-closure glaucoma. Do NOT use topical corticosteroids, and never pad or patch the eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: How is stromal/disciform HSV keratitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Topical corticosteroid PLUS antiviral cover, under ophthalmology supervision — because it is immune-mediated, steroids are needed, but always with antiviral cover.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What prophylaxis is used for recurrent HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Long-term oral aciclovir prophylaxis (reduces recurrence). Also UV protection (sunglasses).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is the role of corneal transplant (keratoplasty) in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: For significant corneal scarring once the disease is quiescent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What general/preventive measures apply in HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back:
• Stop contact lenses
  • treat lid herpes
  • provide UV protection
  • and give prophylactic oral aciclovir for recurrent disease

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What are the complications of HSV keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back:
• Recurrence (very common)
  • corneal scarring → permanent visual loss (leading cause of corneal blindness)
  • geographic/amoeboid ulcer (especially steroid-induced) → corneal melt/perforation
  • neurotrophic (metaherpetic) keratopathy (poor healing from nerve damage)
  • secondary bacterial infection
  • and stromal neovascularisation

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: What is neurotrophic (metaherpetic) keratopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back: Poor corneal healing resulting from HSV damage to the corneal nerves — a complication of recurrent HSV keratitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.front: How does HSV keratitis differ from herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Acanthamoeba keratitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Herpes Simple.back:
• HSV: dendritic ulcer
  • Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: vesicular rash in V1 + Hutchinson's sign (nose-tip involvement) → pseudodendrites
  • Acanthamoeba: contact-lens wearer with severe pain out of proportion to signs

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is diabetic retinopathy and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: A microvascular complication of diabetes in which chronic hyperglycaemia damages the retinal blood vessels → leakage, ischaemia and ultimately abnormal new-vessel growth. It is a leading cause of blindness in the working-age population (16–64) in the UK, largely preventable and detectable early by screening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the core mechanism of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Persistent hyperglycaemia damages the retinal capillary endothelium and pericytes → vessels become leaky (haemorrhages, exudates, oedema) and occluded (retinal ischaemia). Ischaemic retina releases VEGF → neovascularisation (fragile new vessels that bleed and scar).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: Why is every diabetic screened for retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Because it is asymptomatic until it threatens sight, but its sight-threatening stages (proliferative and maculopathy) are treatable if caught in time.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: Why are retinopathy (R) and maculopathy (M) graded on separate axes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Because maculopathy threatens central vision independently of the retinopathy stage.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the features of R1 (background/non-proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Microaneurysms
  • dot/blot haemorrhages
  • and hard exudates.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the features of R2 (pre-proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Venous beading (and venous loops or reduplication)
  • IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities)
  • and multiple deep blot haemorrhages.
Cotton-wool spots often accompany these and signal ischaemia, but on their own they do not upgrade a fundus to R2.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What defines R3 (proliferative) retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: New vessels — at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) — the sight-threatening stage requiring urgent referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What defines M1 (maculopathy)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Exudates, haemorrhage or oedema within about 1 disc diameter of the fovea — the commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes. Maculopathy is graded on its own axis, so every report gives both an R and an M grade (M0 = no maculopathy, M1 = maculopathy present), alongside a P grade for previous laser.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the exam shortcut for grading diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Microaneurysms, dot/blot haemorrhages and hard exudates → background (R1)
  • venous beading, IRMA and multiple blot haemorrhages → pre-proliferative (R2)
  • new vessels → proliferative (R3, urgent referral)
  • changes within one disc diameter of the fovea → maculopathy (M1).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the types of diabetic maculopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Focal/diffuse exudative maculopathy (leakage causing exudates and oedema) and ischaemic maculopathy (macular capillary non-perfusion — poorer prognosis, and poorly responsive to injections). Treatment is decided not by type but by whether the oedema involves the centre of the macula on OCT: centre-involving versus non-centre-involving (the older clinical term was clinically significant macular oedema, CSMO).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the biggest risk factor for diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Duration of diabetes — most type 1 diabetics have some retinopathy after ~20 years.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: List the risk factors for diabetic retinopathy.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Duration of diabetes (biggest)
  • poor glycaemic control (high HbA1c)
  • hypertension
  • hyperlipidaemia
  • pregnancy (can accelerate rapidly — extra screening at booking, at 16–20 weeks if retinopathy is present, and at 28 weeks)
  • renal disease
  • and smoking.
Note type 2 diabetes may already show retinopathy at diagnosis, because hyperglycaemia often predates the diagnosis by years.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is an important warning about rapidly tightening glucose control?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: It can cause transient early worsening of retinopathy — warn patients.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the clinical features of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Asymptomatic in early stages (hence screening)
  • gradual reduction in visual acuity (especially maculopathy affecting central/reading vision)
  • floaters or sudden visual loss suggesting vitreous haemorrhage (from proliferative new vessels)
  • and distortion from maculopathy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the UK Diabetic Eye Screening Programme?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Digital retinal photography through dilated pupils, offered to everyone with diabetes from age 12. Screening is annual by default; in England, people with no retinopathy (R0M0) in both eyes at two consecutive screens are invited every 2 years, while anyone with any retinopathy stays on annual screening. Women with gestational diabetes are not screened.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for macular oedema in diabetes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: OCT — it quantifies retinal thickening to detect and monitor macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the role of fundus fluorescein angiography in diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: It maps ischaemia and neovascularisation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the referral timelines for diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• R3 (proliferative) → urgent (~2 weeks)
  • M1 (maculopathy) or R2 (pre-proliferative) → routine ophthalmology referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What systemic management applies to all diabetic retinopathy patients?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Optimise glycaemic control (individualised HbA1c, e.g. ~48–53 mmol/mol)
  • blood pressure control (type 1: below 135/85, or 130/80 with albuminuria; type 2: below 140/90 in under-80s)
  • lipid management with a statin
  • smoking cessation
  • and additional retinal screening in pregnancy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the first-line treatment for proliferative (R3) diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — laser burns to the peripheral ischaemic retina ablate VEGF-producing tissue so new vessels regress.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the side effects of pan-retinal photocoagulation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Permanent loss of some peripheral visual field, reduced night vision and contrast sensitivity, transient blurring, and possible worsening of macular oedema — PRP deliberately sacrifices peripheral retina to save central vision. Because of the field loss, anyone who has had laser to both eyes must tell the DVLA and may need a binocular visual field test to keep their licence.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the second-line/adjunct treatments for proliferative retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Anti-VEGF (second-line if active despite complete PRP)
  • vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the first-line treatment for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab), given where OCT shows a central retinal thickness of 400 µm or more; below that threshold anti-VEGF or macular laser may be used (NICE). Anti-VEGF is avoided in pregnancy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is the treatment for non-centre-involving diabetic macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Macular laser (the default). Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant) are an option, with cataract/IOP risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What are the complications of diabetic retinopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Vitreous haemorrhage (sudden visual loss/floaters)
  • tractional retinal detachment (fibrous scaffolding contracts)
  • neovascular glaucoma (iris/angle neovascularisation — 'rubeosis iridis')
  • and permanent visual loss/blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: What is rubeosis iridis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back: Neovascularisation of the iris/angle in advanced diabetic retinopathy, which causes neovascular glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.front: How do diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy signs differ on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Diabetic Reti.back:
• Diabetes: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, neovascularisation.
  • Hypertension: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, copper/silver wiring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is chronic open-angle glaucoma (COAG/POAG)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A progressive optic neuropathy — characteristic optic-nerve-head damage with corresponding visual field loss — usually (not always) associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It is the commonest glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is COAG described as a disease 'found by screening'?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Because it is asymptomatic until advanced — painless, gradual peripheral field loss the patient doesn't notice until central vision is threatened — so early detection (optometrist/screening) plus IOP-lowering prevents blindness, but damage already done is permanent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the core mechanism of COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: There is increased resistance to aqueous outflow through an anatomically OPEN angle → IOP rises (or the nerve is susceptible even at 'normal' pressure) → pressure damages retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic nerve head → disc cupping + arcuate/peripheral field defects.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: How does COAG differ from acute angle-closure glaucoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• COAG: open angle, chronic/insidious, painless, white eye, gradual PERIPHERAL field loss, mildly-moderately raised IOP, detected on screening
  • AACG: closed angle, sudden emergency, severe pain, red eye, sudden loss with haloes, very high IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the risk factors for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Increasing age (dominant)
  • raised IOP (major modifiable risk)
  • family history (first-degree relative — strong)
  • Black/African-Caribbean ethnicity (earlier, more aggressive)
  • myopia
  • diabetes
  • hypertension
  • and corticosteroid use (steroid-responders).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Which ethnicity is at higher risk of COAG (and how does this contrast with angle-closure)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Black/African-Caribbean people develop COAG earlier and more aggressively; by contrast, angle-closure glaucoma is commoner in East Asians.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the major MODIFIABLE risk factor for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Raised intraocular pressure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is COAG asymptomatic in early disease?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Because it causes gradual, painless loss of PERIPHERAL vision that patients don't notice, with central vision preserved until late — so it is often detected only on a routine optician visit.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the characteristic pattern of visual loss in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Gradual, painless loss of PERIPHERAL vision progressing to 'tunnel vision' in advanced disease, with central vision preserved until late (the opposite of AMD).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the diagnostic triad of COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• (1) Raised IOP (though normal-tension glaucoma exists)
  • (2) optic disc cupping (increased cup-to-disc ratio)
  • (3) visual field defects.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What optic disc changes are seen in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Increased cup-to-disc ratio (≥0.6, or asymmetry)
  • neuroretinal rim thinning
  • vessel 'bayoneting'
  • notching
  • and disc haemorrhages.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What visual field defects occur in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Arcuate scotomas and a nasal step, progressing to peripheral constriction (tunnel vision).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is normal-tension glaucoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Typical glaucomatous optic nerve damage and field loss occurring at a 'normal' IOP — a recognised variant of COAG where the nerve is susceptible even at normal pressures.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the standard test to measure IOP in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Goldmann applanation tonometry.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the role of gonioscopy in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: It confirms the angle is OPEN, distinguishing COAG from angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What investigations are used in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Goldmann applanation tonometry (IOP)
  • gonioscopy (open angle)
  • visual field testing/perimetry (maps and monitors field loss)
  • optic nerve assessment (fundoscopy/OCT of disc and retinal nerve fibre layer)
  • and central corneal thickness (pachymetry).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: Why is central corneal thickness (pachymetry) measured in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A thin cornea underestimates the true IOP and is also an independent risk factor for glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the aim of COAG treatment?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: To lower IOP to slow/halt progression and preserve remaining vision — damage already done is irreversible.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the first-line treatment for newly diagnosed COAG (NICE)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) — a major recent change (NICE). Laser to the trabecular meshwork improves outflow and can delay or avoid eye drops, removing the daily burden and the adherence problem. Also offered for ocular hypertension with IOP ≥24 mmHg. A generic prostaglandin analogue is offered instead if the patient declines SLT, is waiting for it, or SLT is unsuitable — as in pigment dispersion syndrome. The exception is COAG that is already ADVANCED at diagnosis: laser and drops are bypassed and primary trabeculectomy with mitomycin C is offered.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the first-line DRUG (drop) for COAG and its mechanism?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: A prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) — increases uveoscleral outflow; once-daily. Used if SLT is declined, awaited or unsuitable (for example pigment dispersion syndrome), or as an add-on.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the side effects of latanoprost (prostaglandin analogue)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Iris/periocular pigmentation
  • eyelash growth
  • and conjunctival hyperaemia.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What are the other classes of IOP-lowering drops in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Beta-blocker (timolol — reduces production; contraindicated in asthma and in obstructive airways disease, bradycardia or heart block, because enough is absorbed systemically to cause bronchospasm)
  • carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (dorzolamide; oral acetazolamide — reduces production)
  • alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine — reduces production + increases outflow)
  • and miotics (pilocarpine — increases outflow, less used).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What surgical options exist for COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Trabeculectomy (creates a new drainage channel — a guarded fistula to a subconjunctival 'bleb') for advanced/uncontrolled disease
  • and MIGS (minimally invasive glaucoma surgery)/drainage tubes/shunts, increasingly used.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What monitoring and general measures apply in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back:
• Lifelong follow-up (IOP, visual fields, disc/OCT)
  • screening first-degree relatives
  • and reporting significant field loss to the DVLA (driving).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: What is the key prognostic point about vision loss in COAG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: Vision loss is IRREVERSIBLE — treatment prevents further loss but cannot restore what is lost. Hence lifelong monitoring and screening of relatives.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.front: How does COAG contrast with AMD in the pattern of vision loss?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Chronic Open-.back: COAG causes peripheral (tunnel) loss with central vision preserved until late; AMD causes central vision loss with preserved peripheral vision — opposite patterns.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Thrombotic occlusion of the central retinal vein → blockage of venous drainage → back-pressure causing widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema and (if severe) ischaemia. It is a common cause of sudden painless visual loss in older adults and is the venous counterpart to CRAO.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does the core mechanism of CRVO contrast with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• CRAO is arterial (no blood IN → pale retina) and is managed as a stroke — emergency same-day referral onto the stroke pathway.
  • CRVO is venous (blood cannot get OUT → back-pressure → the retina engorges, haemorrhages and swells) and is an urgent ophthalmology referral, seen within about a week — same day if a painful red eye with very high pressure or iris new vessels suggests neovascular glaucoma.
It is not a stroke-pathway emergency.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does CRVO share arterial risk factors despite being a venous event?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The thrombus forms where the central retinal vein shares a sheath with the stiff atherosclerotic central retinal artery at the lamina cribrosa — so hypertension and atherosclerosis are risk factors.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the two types of CRVO and their relative frequency?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Non-ischaemic (~75%) — milder, better vision (often >6/60), absent/mild RAPD, <10 disc areas of non-perfusion
  • and ischaemic (~25%) — severe, poor vision (often <6/60), marked RAPD, >10 disc areas of non-perfusion.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does the ischaemic-vs-non-ischaemic distinction matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The ischaemic type drives VEGF release → neovascularisation of the iris/angle → neovascular glaucoma ('90-day glaucoma') + vitreous haemorrhage. Non-ischaemic CRVO can also convert to ischaemic, so all need monitoring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Roughly what proportion of non-ischaemic CRVO converts to ischaemic?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: About a third, over roughly three years — which is why every non-ischaemic CRVO needs ongoing monitoring rather than discharge.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the commonest risk factor for CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Hypertension (with atherosclerosis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: List the risk factors for CRVO.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Increasing age (>50)
  • hypertension (commonest)
  • hyperlipidaemia
  • diabetes
  • smoking
  • raised intraocular pressure/glaucoma (a specific CRVO risk)
  • hyperviscosity/thrombophilia (polycythaemia, myeloma, antiphospholipid syndrome)
  • inflammatory/vasculitic causes (Behçet's, sarcoidosis)
  • and the oral contraceptive pill (younger patients).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Which CRVO risk factor is specific to the eye rather than systemic vasculature?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Raised intraocular pressure/glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: When should hyperviscosity/thrombophilia causes be considered in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
In younger patients, or bilateral/recurrent cases — consider
  • polycythaemia
  • myeloma
  • antiphospholipid syndrome
  • protein C/S deficiency and autoimmune/inflammatory causes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the typical presentation of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden, painless loss/blurring of vision in ONE eye, of variable severity (mild blurring to profound loss), often noticed on waking (venous stasis overnight).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What pupillary sign indicates ischaemic CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A marked relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — a marker of severity.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the classic fundoscopic picture of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
A 'blood and thunder' fundus (also called 'stormy sunset') —
  • widespread flame and blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants (hallmark)
  • dilated, tortuous veins
  • cotton-wool spots
  • optic disc swelling
  • and macular oedema.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) differ from CRVO on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• BRVO: haemorrhages confined to one sector/quadrant drained by the blocked branch, classically at an arteriovenous crossing.
  • CRVO: haemorrhages in all four quadrants.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How is CRVO diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Largely clinically on fundoscopy/slit-lamp, supported by OCT (quantifies macular oedema) and fundus fluorescein angiography (assesses capillary non-perfusion to classify ischaemic vs non-ischaemic, best once haemorrhage clears).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the role of OCT in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It quantifies macular oedema — key for guiding and monitoring treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the role of fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It assesses capillary non-perfusion to classify ischaemic vs non-ischaemic CRVO (best done once the haemorrhage clears).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What systemic work-up is done in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• BP
  • fasting glucose/HbA1c
  • lipids
  • FBC (polycythaemia/hyperviscosity)
  • ESR
  • and intraocular pressure.
In young/bilateral/recurrent cases, add a thrombophilia and inflammatory screen (antiphospholipid, protein C/S, myeloma, autoimmune).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the first-line/gold-standard treatment for CRVO macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections — ranibizumab, aflibercept or faricimab (bevacizumab is also used, but off-label, as it has no ophthalmic licence). They improve vision and reduce oedema, and early treatment gives better outcomes. Nothing reopens the occluded vein — treatment targets the consequences.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the second-line/adjunct treatment for CRVO macular oedema, and its risks?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Intravitreal steroids (dexamethasone implant/triamcinolone) — with the risks of cataract and raised IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Is macular grid laser recommended for CRVO macular oedema?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: No — unlike in BRVO, macular grid laser is NOT recommended for CRVO macular oedema: it reduces leakage on angiography but gives no visual benefit.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How is neovascularisation / ischaemic CRVO treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) — laser to ablate ischaemic retina, reducing the VEGF drive, for neovascularisation of the iris/angle/retina (prevents/treats neovascular glaucoma); anti-VEGF is a useful adjunct.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How closely should ischaemic CRVO be monitored, and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Monthly review for the first 6 months — the risk of iris and angle new vessels is highest in the first 90 days ("90-day glaucoma"). Examine the iris and check intraocular pressure at every visit, then review less frequently once past the high-risk period.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What systemic management is important in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Treat cardiovascular risk factors — control BP, lipids and diabetes, and support smoking cessation — to reduce risk to the fellow eye, and address any hyperviscosity, thrombophilia or inflammatory cause in younger patients. CRVO is a marker of systemic vascular disease. Note that aspirin, other antiplatelets and anticoagulants are NOT indicated to treat the CRVO itself, unlike CRAO where aspirin and stroke secondary prevention are central; continue them only if already prescribed for another reason.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the complications of CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Macular oedema (commonest cause of visual loss)
  • neovascular glaucoma (from iris/angle neovascularisation in the ischaemic type — painful, sight-threatening, '90-day glaucoma')
  • vitreous haemorrhage
  • tractional retinal detachment
  • and macular ischaemia (permanent central loss).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is 'neovascular glaucoma' / '90-day glaucoma' in CRVO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Neovascular glaucoma from iris/angle neovascularisation driven by ischaemia, classically developing around 90 days after ischaemic CRVO — a painful, sight-threatening complication.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden occlusion of the central retinal artery → acute ischaemia of the inner retina → sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye. It is a 'stroke of the eye' and a warning of imminent stroke and cardiovascular events.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why has the modern emphasis in CRAO shifted, given vision is often lost permanently?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Towards treating the patient as a stroke (urgent work-up + secondary prevention) and not missing giant cell arteritis (treatable → saves the other eye).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What part of the retina does the central retinal artery supply, and what is its origin?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It supplies the INNER retina. It is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which is the first branch of the internal carotid artery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: Why does the fovea show a 'cherry-red spot' in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: The inner retina infarcts and becomes pale/oedematous, but the fovea is thin and shows the underlying choroidal circulation through it, appearing as a cherry-red spot against the pale retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the two types of CRAO and their relative frequency?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Non-arteritic (~>95%) — embolus/thrombosis (carotid atheroma, cardiac)
  • and arteritic (<5%) — giant cell arteritis (± other vasculitides).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What clues suggest ARTERITIC CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
Age >50 with
  • headache
  • jaw claudication
  • scalp tenderness
  • polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms
  • and raised ESR/CRP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the action for arteritic CRAO and why is it urgent?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Immediate high-dose corticosteroids (don't wait for biopsy) — to protect/save the fellow eye, as missing it risks rapid, bilateral, irreversible blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What must always be asked/checked in any patient over 50 with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Ask about GCA symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR) and check ESR/CRP — missing arteritic CRAO risks rapid bilateral blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the commonest embolic source in non-arteritic CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Carotid artery atherosclerosis (calcific/cholesterol emboli).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What cardiac sources can cause CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• AF
  • valvular disease
  • endocarditis
  • and post-MI mural thrombus.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: List the vascular risk factors for non-arteritic CRAO.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Hypertension
  • diabetes
  • hyperlipidaemia
  • smoking
  • hypercoagulable states
  • vasculitis
  • and sickle cell disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the classic presentation of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Sudden, painless, severe loss of vision in ONE eye — often 'counting fingers' or worse, and may be complete.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What may precede CRAO and what does it suggest?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Amaurosis fugax — transient 'curtain' visual loss — which suggests a carotid embolic source.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What pupillary sign is found in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — the affected pupil dilates on the swinging-light test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• A pale, oedematous ('whitened') retina with a cherry-red spot at the fovea (classic)
  • attenuated (thread-like) arteries
  • segmentation of the blood column ('cattle-trucking')
  • and sometimes a visible embolus (Hollenhorst plaque) at a bifurcation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is a Hollenhorst plaque?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: A visible cholesterol embolus seen at a retinal arterial bifurcation, indicating a carotid embolic source.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What urgent blood tests are done in CRAO and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Urgent ESR and CRP in anyone over 50, to exclude giant cell arteritis. Confirm afterwards with temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) and/or temporal artery biopsy, ideally within 1 week of starting steroids and not beyond 2 weeks — skip lesions mean a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA. Never delay steroids for either test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What further investigations form the 'stroke-like' work-up of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• FBC, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, clotting
  • ECG (AF) and carotid Doppler ultrasound (carotid stenosis)
  • echocardiogram if a cardiac source is suspected
  • OCT (retinal oedema) and fundus fluorescein angiography (delayed arterial filling) to confirm
  • brain imaging as part of the stroke pathway
  • and BP/vascular risk assessment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the first management priority in a patient over 50 with CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Exclude and treat giant cell arteritis. If GCA is suspected, give immediate high-dose corticosteroid before any biopsy — with visual loss already present that means IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g daily for up to 3 days, then high-dose oral prednisolone (high-dose oral alone is for GCA without visual or ischaemic symptoms). The aim is to protect the fellow eye, which is at risk within days.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What acute 'eye' measures may be attempted in CRAO (and their evidence level)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• Ocular massage (intermittent digital globe pressure to dislodge an embolus)
  • lowering IOP with IV acetazolamide ± mannitol, or anterior chamber paracentesis (an ophthalmologist-only procedure, not something to attempt yourself)
  • and rebreathing into a paper bag or inhaled carbogen (CO2 → retinal vasodilation).
All are low-evidence and none is proven to restore vision — do them only while the emergency referral is being made, never instead of it. Systemic vasodilators such as GTN are not recommended, because dropping the blood pressure reduces ocular perfusion pressure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the current role of thrombolysis in CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: It is NOT standard care. Randomised trials of IV thrombolysis given within 4.5 hours found no better visual outcome than oral aspirin, and one found serious safety concerns including intracranial haemorrhage, major bleeding and death — so it belongs only in a trial or on specialist stroke-team advice. The lasting message from those trials is the pathway, not the drug: assess and work the patient up as an acute stroke, with aspirin 300 mg unless contraindicated.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the most important long-term step in CRAO management?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
Secondary prevention — treat as a TIA/stroke:
  • aspirin 300 mg immediately, then long-term antiplatelet (clopidogrel 75 mg daily first-line)
  • carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis, aiming within 14 days
  • anticoagulate AF
  • high-intensity statin
  • control BP, diabetes and lipids
  • smoking cessation.
This prevents the next cerebral stroke or MI — the real threat to the patient.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What are the ocular complications of CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Permanent visual loss (usual outcome — ~80% counting-fingers or worse), and ocular neovascularisation (retinal ischaemia drives VEGF) → neovascular glaucoma and vitreous haemorrhage → follow up ~monthly for up to ~4 months.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the systemic danger after CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Subsequent stroke or MI — the real threat to the patient, which is why secondary prevention is the priority.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: How does CRAO differ from central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) on fundoscopy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back:
• CRAO: pale oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot.
  • CRVO: the venous counterpart — a 'blood and thunder' fundus (widespread haemorrhages), not a pale retina.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.front: What is the differential for a cherry-red spot besides CRAO?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Central Retin.back: Storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs in infants (CRAO is in the elderly and acute).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a cataract and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: An opacification (clouding) of the normally transparent crystalline lens. It is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and the commonest treatable cause of visual impairment; cataract surgery is the most frequently performed NHS operation and one of the most successful in medicine.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the core mechanism of cataract formation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The lens is normally kept clear by orderly proteins (crystallins). With ageing and oxidative stress (or metabolic/toxic insults), these proteins denature and aggregate, scattering light → the lens clouds → light can't focus cleanly on the retina → blurred vision, glare and dimmed colours.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the commonest type/cause of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Age-related (senile) cataract — from ageing and oxidative stress.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the secondary causes of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
• Diabetes
  • corticosteroids
  • trauma
  • uveitis
  • radiation
  • high myopia
  • and previous eye surgery.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What causes congenital cataract, and how is it detected?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
Detected early by an absent red reflex (newborn/6-week check). Causes include
  • intrauterine infection (rubella)
  • galactosaemia
  • Down syndrome
  • and hereditary causes.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a nuclear sclerotic cataract and its characteristic effect?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The commonest age-related type, affecting the central lens; it causes a myopic shift ('second sight' — some elderly people transiently read without glasses).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a cortical cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Spoke-like wedge opacities from the lens periphery; prominent glare.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is a posterior subcapsular cataract and its associations?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Opacity at the back of the lens, associated with steroids and diabetes; causes disproportionate glare and near-vision difficulty and progresses faster.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the dominant risk factor for cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Increasing age.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: List the risk factors for cataract.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
• Increasing age (dominant)
  • smoking and high alcohol intake
  • diabetes mellitus/metabolic disorders
  • corticosteroids (systemic or topical — the classic drug cause)
  • UV/sunlight
  • ionising radiation
  • ocular trauma
  • previous intraocular surgery
  • uveitis
  • high myopia
  • and congenital/hereditary causes/intrauterine infection.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: Which drug class is the classic drug cause of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Corticosteroids (systemic or topical) — associated with posterior subcapsular cataract.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the typical clinical features of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
• Gradual, painless loss/blurring of vision over months–years
  • glare (bright lights, night headlights, haloes)
  • faded/yellowed colours
  • reduced contrast sensitivity
  • occasionally monocular diplopia
  • myopic shift (nuclear)
  • usually bilateral but asymmetric.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the key examination sign of cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Loss of the red reflex (or a dark opacity silhouetted against it). The lens may look cloudy/grey when advanced.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What does an absent red reflex in a neonate indicate, and what must be done?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: An absent red reflex, or a white pupil (leukocoria), is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise — congenital cataract is the commoner cause, but both need urgent same-day referral. It is checked at the newborn and 6-week examinations.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: How is cataract diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Clinically — visual acuity + slit-lamp examination (grades and localises the cataract) + red reflex/ophthalmoscopy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What pre-operative assessment is needed before cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Biometry (measures the eye to calculate the intraocular lens power) and assessment for co-existing eye disease (glaucoma, AMD, diabetic retinopathy) that would limit visual benefit.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What investigations are needed for a congenital cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
Investigate the cause —
  • TORCH screen
  • galactosaemia testing
  • and a metabolic/genetic work-up.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: Is there any medical treatment that reverses or halts cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: No — surgery is the only cure. Interim measures (stronger glasses, brighter reading lights) may help mild cataract, plus modifying risk factors (stop smoking, glycaemic control).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is the definitive surgical treatment for cataract?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Phacoemulsification — ultrasound emulsifies and aspirates the cloudy lens through a small incision, and an artificial intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted. Usually a day-case under local anaesthetic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is given during cataract surgery to prevent endophthalmitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Intracameral cefuroxime.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What are the NICE referral criteria for cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: Do NOT restrict access on visual acuity alone. Offer surgery when the cataract affects quality of life (after discussing risks/benefits) — a functional decision, not a fixed acuity cut-off. Second-eye surgery uses the same criteria.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is endophthalmitis and how does it present after cataract surgery?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: A rare but serious intraocular infection — a painful red eye with visual loss days after surgery. It is a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: What is posterior capsule opacification (PCO) and how is it treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back: The commonest late complication ('secondary cataract'): the capsule behind the IOL clouds months–years after surgery. Treated with YAG laser capsulotomy (quick and effective).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.front: List the complications of cataract surgery.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Cataracts.back:
• Endophthalmitis (emergency)
  • posterior capsule opacification (commonest late → YAG laser)
  • posterior capsule rupture (intraoperative)
  • retinal detachment
  • cystoid macular oedema
  • IOL dislocation
  • and raised IOP.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is bacterial conjunctivitis and where does it sit among red-eye causes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: A bacterial infection of the conjunctiva — one of the three common causes of the 'red eye' (with viral and allergic). It is very common and mostly benign/self-limiting, but a few presentations are sight- or life-threatening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: In acute infective conjunctivitis, which presentations must you not miss?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Recognising that most cases are a self-limiting nuisance, and spotting the minority that is sight- or life-threatening (gonococcal, chlamydial, neonatal, contact-lens-related) — while reassuring the rest.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does the discharge differ between bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Bacterial: purulent, sticky (yellow-green), lids stuck together on waking
  • Viral: watery
  • Allergic: watery/stringy with prominent itch

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does laterality differ between bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Bacterial: often starts unilateral then spreads
  • Viral: often bilateral (one then the other)
  • Allergic: bilateral

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: Which features are shared by bacterial, viral and allergic conjunctivitis — and what does their absence mean?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Red eye
  • normal vision
  • no significant pain
  • no photophobia
  • normal pupil
If any of these is absent → think keratitis, uveitis, scleritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma instead.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the common causative organisms of bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Staphylococcus aureus
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Haemophilus influenzae (especially in children)
  • and Moraxella

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: Which organism is the classic cause of contact-lens-related eye infection, and why does it matter?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Gram-negative) — high risk of keratitis/corneal ulcer; Acanthamoeba is another contact-lens-associated cause. These threaten sight.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the features of gonococcal conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Hyperacute onset with copious purulent discharge, rapidly sight-threatening (corneal perforation) — caused by N. gonorrhoeae.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the features of chlamydial conjunctivitis, and its global significance?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Chronic/subacute conjunctivitis caused by C. trachomatis; trachoma (serotypes A–C) is the world's leading infective cause of blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the classic clinical features of bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: A red, gritty, 'sore' eye (foreign-body sensation, not true pain) with purulent/mucopurulent discharge; eyelids crusted/stuck together in the morning; discharge re-accumulates within minutes of wiping. Usually starts in one eye and spreads; vision normal, no significant pain/photophobia, pupil normal; diffuse conjunctival injection toward the fornices.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is bacterial conjunctivitis usually diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Clinically — history and examination; no tests for routine cases.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: When are swabs (MC&S + chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT) indicated in conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: For severe/hyperacute cases, suspected gonococcal/chlamydial infection, neonatal conjunctivitis, contact-lens wearers, the immunocompromised, or treatment failure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: When is fluorescein staining used in suspected conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: If corneal involvement is suspected — to rule out an ulcer/keratitis, especially in contact-lens wearers.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the first-line management of routine bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
Supportive care:
  • reassurance (most resolve within 5–7 days without treatment)
  • bathing/cleaning lids with cotton wool and cooled boiled water/saline to remove crusts
  • and hygiene measures
Antibiotics are often unnecessary.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What hygiene advice is given in bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Hand-washing
  • don't share towels/pillows (it is contagious)
  • avoid eye-rubbing and contact lenses until resolved
School/work exclusion is not routinely required (UKHSA).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the first-line topical antibiotic for bacterial conjunctivitis, and how can it be prescribed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Chloramphenicol (0.5% drops / 1% ointment) — broad-spectrum, and buyable from a pharmacy without prescription for adults and children aged 2 years and over (younger children need medical assessment). A delayed prescription (start if not improving after ~3 days) is reasonable.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is the alternative topical antibiotic to chloramphenicol, and when is it useful?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Fusidic acid — an alternative (no Gram-negative cover), useful in pregnancy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What are the cautions with chloramphenicol?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Avoid after previous myelosuppression or a blood dyscrasia. In pregnancy it is generally avoided where possible (fusidic acid is the usual topical alternative) — remembering that most cases need no antibiotic at all.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How should a contact-lens wearer with a red eye be managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Stop lens wear and refer — same-day if there is pain, photophobia or reduced vision — to exclude microbial keratitis (Pseudomonas/Acanthamoeba), which is sight-threatening. Never patch the eye, and ask the patient to bring their lenses and case.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is gonococcal conjunctivitis treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Systemic ceftriaxone plus urgent ophthalmology referral (it is hyperacute and sight-threatening).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How is chlamydial conjunctivitis treated?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Systemic doxycycline is first-line (azithromycin if doxycycline is unsuitable, for example in pregnancy), plus GUM referral and contact tracing, because it is an STI. Topical treatment alone is inadequate.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: What is ophthalmia neonatorum and how is it managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back: Neonatal conjunctivitis in the first 28 days of life — gonococcal (typically within 48 h, hyperacute and sight-threatening) or chlamydial (5–14 days), acquired from the maternal genital tract. It always needs urgent same-day paediatric/ophthalmology assessment with eye swabs (Gram stain, culture and chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT) and systemic antibiotics — never treat a neonate with over-the-counter chloramphenicol and review later. The mother and her partner need testing and treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.front: How does bacterial conjunctivitis differ from viral conjunctivitis on associated features?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Bacterial Con.back:
• Viral is watery with a preauricular lymph node, follicles, and a recent URTI
  • bacterial has purulent sticky discharge and lacks these viral associations

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is allergic conjunctivitis and what hypersensitivity mechanism underlies it?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity inflammation of the conjunctiva in response to an allergen. It is extremely common, often alongside allergic rhinitis ('hay fever eyes').

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: Describe the mechanism of allergic conjunctivitis.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Allergen contacts the conjunctiva → binds IgE on mast cells → degranulation → histamine release → itch, redness, watering and swelling. This is why antihistamines (block the effect) and mast-cell stabilisers (prevent the release) are the treatments.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the hallmark symptom of allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Itch — prominent and the most specific symptom; both eyes are typically affected, watery and red.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What features are NOT part of allergic conjunctivitis and should prompt exclusion of a dangerous red eye?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back:
• Significant pain
  • marked photophobia
  • reduced vision
  • or an abnormal pupil
— their presence means you must exclude keratitis, anterior uveitis, scleritis or acute angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How does the discharge and laterality of allergic conjunctivitis compare with bacterial conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back:
• Allergic: bilateral, watery/stringy mucoid discharge, prominent itch
  • Bacterial: often unilateral (or spreads), purulent discharge, less itch

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is seasonal allergic conjunctivitis (SAC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: The commonest type — caused by pollen (grass, tree), occurring in spring/summer ('hay fever'), often with allergic rhinitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is perennial allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A year-round form caused by house dust mite, animal dander or mould.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A more severe, chronic form in children/young males, with large 'cobblestone' giant papillae under the upper lid; it can threaten sight (corneal involvement) and needs specialist care.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: A chronic, sight-threatening form in adults with atopic dermatitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is giant papillary conjunctivitis associated with?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Contact lenses, sutures or ocular prostheses.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is chemosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Conjunctival oedema — a swollen, 'boggy', sometimes gelatinous conjunctiva — a characteristic sign of allergic conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What are the typical clinical features of allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back:
• Bilateral itching (dominant)
  • watery/stringy mucoid discharge
  • red injected conjunctiva
  • chemosis
  • eyelid swelling
  • tearing
  • and often associated rhinitis and personal/family atopy (asthma, eczema, hay fever)
Papillae ('cobblestones') may be seen on lid eversion, especially in VKC.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How is allergic conjunctivitis diagnosed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Clinically — history (itch, bilateral, atopy, seasonality) and examination are usually sufficient. No routine tests are needed.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When might allergy testing (skin-prick/RAST) be considered in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: If the trigger is unclear or symptoms are severe/persistent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When should allergic conjunctivitis be referred?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain, red flags are present, or a severe/sight-threatening form (VKC/atopic keratoconjunctivitis) is suspected.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What are the first, non-pharmacological management steps for allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back:
• Allergen avoidance (the foundation)
  • cool compresses
  • artificial tears/lubricants (to dilute and wash out allergen and soothe)
  • avoiding eye rubbing
  • and avoiding contact lenses during flares

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the first-line topical drug treatment for allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Topical antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine, ketotifen — many are dual-action antihistamine + mast-cell stabiliser) — giving rapid relief, good for acute/intermittent symptoms.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How do topical mast-cell stabilisers work and what is their key limitation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Sodium cromoglicate (the UK mainstay, available over the counter) and lodoxamide prevent mast-cell degranulation — prophylactic — but they do NOT relieve established symptoms and take days–weeks to work, so start them BEFORE the season and use them regularly through it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: What is the key distinction between antihistamines and mast-cell stabilisers in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back:
• Antihistamines RELIEVE established symptoms rapidly
  • mast-cell stabilisers PREVENT symptoms but don't relieve them and are slow-onset — so they must be started early

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When are oral antihistamines used in allergic conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: When there is associated allergic rhinitis or systemic allergy (cetirizine, loratadine).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: When are topical corticosteroids used in allergic conjunctivitis, and what are the risks?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: Only for severe/resistant disease and under specialist/ophthalmology supervision — because of the risks of raised IOP/glaucoma, cataract, and worsening herpetic keratitis. Never prescribe steroid drops for a red eye without excluding these.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.front: How are vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Allergic Conj.back: With specialist care — topical steroids and ciclosporin — because they are chronic and sight-threatening.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Progressive degeneration of the macula — the central retina responsible for high-acuity central vision — and the leading cause of irreversible visual loss in older adults in the developed world.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What vision does AMD affect and what does it spare?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It robs CENTRAL vision (reading, driving, recognising faces) while sparing PERIPHERAL vision — so patients are rarely completely blind.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What structures does AMD damage at the macula?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), Bruch's membrane and photoreceptors at the macula.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are drusen and their significance?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Yellow deposits of metabolic waste that accumulate at the macula — the hallmark of AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the frequency and mechanism of DRY (atrophic) AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: ~85–90% of cases. Gradual RPE/photoreceptor atrophy with drusen; late disease is geographic atrophy. Driven by oxidative stress and ageing.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the frequency and mechanism of WET (neovascular) AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: ~10–15% of cases. Choroidal neovascularisation — abnormal vessels grow from the choroid through Bruch's membrane and leak/bleed. Driven by VEGF.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How does the onset differ between dry and wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
• Dry: gradual over years, slow progressive loss
  • Wet: rapid (days–weeks) with sudden central loss/distortion — responsible for ~90% of severe visual loss in AMD

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the key clinical instinct for wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: An elderly patient with SUDDEN central visual distortion → suspect wet AMD → urgent referral (there is a treatable window). Gradual bilateral central blurring over years suggests dry AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the biggest MODIFIABLE risk factor for AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Smoking — strongly linked and the biggest modifiable risk.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: List the risk factors for AMD.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
• Increasing age (dominant)
  • smoking (biggest modifiable)
  • family history/genetics (complement factor H polymorphisms)
  • Caucasian ethnicity
  • hypertension/cardiovascular disease
  • poor diet (low antioxidants)
  • and female sex

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is metamorphopsia and how is it tested?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Straight lines appearing wavy/distorted — a classic symptom (especially wet AMD), tested with an Amsler grid.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is a central scotoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: A blank/dark central patch in the visual field — a feature of AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What visual symptoms occur in AMD besides distortion and scotoma?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
• Reduced acuity
  • difficulty reading/recognising faces
  • poor low-light adaptation
  • and micropsia/macropsia (objects appearing smaller/larger)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: Why is preserved peripheral vision important in AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It provides reassurance (patients are not totally blind) and distinguishes AMD from glaucoma (which causes peripheral loss).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in dry AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
• Drusen (yellow macular deposits)
  • RPE pigmentary changes
  • and geographic atrophy in advanced disease

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What are the fundoscopy findings in wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
• Macular haemorrhage
  • exudates
  • fluid/oedema
  • and sometimes a grey-green subretinal (neovascular) membrane

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the KEY investigation in AMD and what does it show?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) — cross-sectional retinal imaging showing fluid (intra-/subretinal), drusen and neovascular membranes; it guides diagnosis and monitors treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the role of fluorescein angiography (FFA) in AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: It confirms and localises choroidal neovascularisation in wet AMD (showing leakage).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the role of the Amsler grid?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: A bedside test (and self-monitoring tool) where the patient reports distorted or missing lines — useful for detecting metamorphopsia and conversion of dry to wet AMD.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How is DRY AMD managed?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back:
No cure to reverse it → supportive measures and slowing progression:
  • smoking cessation (the key modifiable factor)
  • low-vision aids
  • sight-impaired registration
  • Amsler grid self-monitoring to catch conversion to wet AMD
  • and a discussion of antioxidant/zinc eye supplements (not NHS-funded; they may slow intermediate-to-advanced progression)

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the role of antioxidant/zinc eye supplements in AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: High-dose antioxidants (vitamins C and E) with zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin. The evidence suggests they probably slow progression from intermediate to advanced AMD; they do NOT reverse damage and do NOT help early AMD. They are not routinely NHS-funded, so counsel honestly rather than promising benefit. Avoid beta-carotene-containing formulations in smokers.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What new treatments slow geographic atrophy in dry AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Intravitreal complement inhibitors (pegcetacoplan, targeting C3; avacincaptad, targeting C5). They slow the growth of the geographic atrophy lesion but do NOT improve vision. Neither is licensed in the UK and neither is available on the NHS — so in UK practice, advanced dry AMD is still managed supportively.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: What is the mainstay, sight-saving treatment for WET AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections — ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab (and brolucizumab) — which block VEGF to halt neovascularisation and leakage. A loading course then maintenance ('treat-and-extend'/PRN, guided by OCT). Anti-VEGF preserves the remaining vision more than it restores vision already lost.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: Why is referral urgent in suspected wet AMD?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: Because anti-VEGF works best early — it preserves the vision that is left rather than restoring what has been lost. Refer suspected wet AMD to a macular service within 1 working day (NICE); treatment should start within 14 days of referral.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.front: How does AMD differ from glaucoma in the pattern of vision loss?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Age-Related M.back: AMD causes central vision loss with preserved peripheral vision; glaucoma causes peripheral (tunnel) loss with central vision preserved until late — opposite patterns.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG)?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A sight-threatening ophthalmic emergency in which the drainage angle of the anterior chamber becomes suddenly blocked, causing intraocular pressure (IOP) to rise rapidly and severely (often 50–80 mmHg vs normal 10–21). Delayed treatment causes irreversible optic nerve damage and permanent blindness.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the normal range of intraocular pressure, and what is it in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Normal 10–21 mmHg; in AACG it is often 50–80 mmHg (usually >40–50).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Describe the normal flow of aqueous humour.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Aqueous is made by the ciliary body → flows from the posterior chamber → through the pupil → into the anterior chamber → drains via the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the mechanism of pupillary block in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: In a susceptible eye (shallow anterior chamber, narrow angle), the iris bows forward and blocks the pupil ('pupillary block') → aqueous can't pass forward → pressure balloons the iris forward → it seals off the drainage angle → IOP shoots up.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What pupil state most commonly triggers AACG?
