conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Pupil dilation — mid-dilation is worst, as the iris bunches into the angle.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the classic clinical triad of AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Red painful eye
  • reduced vision/haloes around lights
  • nausea and vomiting.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the classic pupil and corneal signs of AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A fixed, mid-dilated, oval, non-reactive pupil, and a hazy/cloudy (oedematous) cornea with reduced red reflex. There is also ciliary injection and a shallow anterior chamber, and the eye may feel hard ('like a marble') on palpation.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Which refractive error is the classic risk factor for AACG and why?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) — small eyes with shallow anterior chambers and narrow angles.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: List the risk factors for AACG.
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Hypermetropia (classic)
  • increasing age (lens thickens/moves forward)
  • female sex
  • Asian ethnicity
  • family history
  • and mydriasis-provoking triggers.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What triggers can provoke AACG via mydriasis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Dim light (cinema/dark room)
  • pupil-dilating drugs (anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics, some antihistamines, and nebulised ipratropium by face mask)
  • and pharmacological dilation for fundoscopy (a classic exam trigger).
Topiramate is the exception — it closes the angle without pupillary block, so the attack is usually bilateral with a myopic shift, and the treatment is to stop the drug rather than iridotomy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why can AACG masquerade as an acute abdomen or migraine?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because vagally-mediated nausea and vomiting may dominate the presentation and mislead, alongside headache — the eye signs can be overlooked.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the key confirmatory investigation in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Tonometry — measuring IOP (often >40–50 mmHg).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the role of gonioscopy in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: It is the specialist test that visualises the drainage angle directly and confirms it is closed — the definitive angle assessment, done by ophthalmology. You are not expected to perform it; you are expected to know it distinguishes angle-closure from open-angle glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why must the fellow (other) eye be assessed in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because it is usually also narrow-angled and predisposed → it needs prophylactic treatment (laser peripheral iridotomy).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the immediate general measures in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Immediate ophthalmology referral
  • start IOP-lowering treatment while awaiting them
  • lie the patient flat, face up (lets the lens fall back)
  • and give analgesia and antiemetics.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the single most useful systemic IOP-lowering agent in AACG, and its cautions?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Acetazolamide 500 mg — a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces aqueous production. Give it IV if the patient is vomiting (which most are), orally only if they can keep it down. Avoid in severe renal impairment, sulfonamide hypersensitivity and hypokalaemia/hyponatraemia; caution in sickle cell disease (BNF).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What topical medical agents are used to lower IOP in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Topical beta-blocker (timolol) — reduces aqueous production, but it is contraindicated in asthma and obstructive airways disease, bradycardia and heart block, because eye drops are absorbed systemically and fatal bronchospasm is documented; use an alternative in those patients
  • Topical alpha-2 agonist (brimonidine/apraclonidine) — reduces production and increases outflow
  • Topical steroid (prednisolone) — reduces the intraocular inflammation, given once the diagnosis is made under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: When is IV mannitol used in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: As an osmotic agent if the IOP is not controlled by other measures.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is pilocarpine's action in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: A miotic — it constricts the pupil, pulling the iris away from the angle to reopen it.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: Why must pilocarpine be timed carefully in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Because it only works once the IOP is lowered: above roughly 40–45 mmHg the iris sphincter is ischaemic and unresponsive, so pilocarpine 2% (4% in a heavily pigmented iris) is given once the pressure has started to fall with acetazolamide and the topical agents. It is also instilled into the fellow eye as prophylaxis pending bilateral laser iridotomy.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is the definitive treatment for AACG, and why is it done in both eyes?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — a small hole in the peripheral iris creates an alternative channel for aqueous to bypass the pupillary block, equalising pressure so the iris falls back and the angle reopens. Performed in BOTH eyes, as the fellow eye is predisposed (prophylaxis).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What is an increasingly used definitive alternative to LPI in AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back: Lens extraction (cataract surgery) — especially where there is co-existing cataract.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: What are the complications of untreated/delayed AACG?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• Permanent visual loss/blindness (optic nerve infarction)
  • optic atrophy
  • central retinal artery or vein occlusion
  • recurrent attacks
  • and chronic angle-closure glaucoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.front: How does AACG differ from primary open-angle glaucoma in presentation?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Acute Angle-C.back:
• AACG: sudden onset, severe pain + headache, red congested eye, acute blurring with haloes, nausea/vomiting, fixed mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP
  • Open-angle: chronic/insidious, painless, white eye, gradual peripheral field loss, normal pupil, mildly-moderately raised IOP.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What do the numerator and denominator of a Snellen fraction (e.g. 6/12) mean?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Numerator = the testing distance in metres (usually 6 m). Denominator = the distance at which a person with normal vision could read that same line. So 6/12 means the patient reads at 6 m what a normal eye reads at 12 m (worse than normal). 6/6 is normal.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What does an improvement in visual acuity through a pinhole indicate?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: That the deficit is due to uncorrected refractive error rather than organic pathology. The pinhole restricts light to the central optical axis, negating refractive blur. If VA does NOT improve, the cause lies in the media, retina or optic nerve and needs investigation.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: How is vision recorded when the patient cannot read the top (6/60) Snellen letter at 6 m?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Step down through: reduced distance (e.g. 3/60), then counting fingers (CF), hand movements (HM), perception of light (PL), and finally no perception of light (NPL). Always document the exact level rather than 'unrecordable'.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What structures does the slit-lamp biomicroscope examine, and what do 'cells and flare' signify?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: It gives a magnified stereoscopic view of the anterior segment: lids, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber, iris and lens (and the fundus with a condensing lens). Cells and flare in the anterior chamber indicate active anterior uveitis (leucocytes and protein from inflammation).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why is LogMAR preferred over Snellen in formal/research settings?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: LogMAR charts have an equal number of letters per line, uniform spacing and a regular logarithmic size progression, making measurements more accurate and reproducible. A lower LogMAR score means better vision (0.0 equals 6/6; negative values are better than normal).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Which hand, eye and scope-hand do you use to examine a patient's RIGHT eye on fundoscopy?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Your RIGHT eye, holding the ophthalmoscope in your RIGHT hand (the 'same-same' rule); reverse for the left eye.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What mydriatic drop is standard for dilated fundoscopy and what is its duration?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Tropicamide 1% — a short-acting mydriatic with onset ~15-20 min lasting 4-6 hours; phenylephrine 2.5% can be added for wider dilation.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What does leukocoria (a white red reflex) in a neonate signify?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Retinoblastoma until proven otherwise (also congenital cataract) — requires urgent same-day ophthalmology referral as it is life-threatening.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What cup:disc ratio findings suggest glaucomatous optic neuropathy?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: A cup:disc ratio of 0.6 or greater, or asymmetry of more than 0.2 between the two eyes.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why must you avoid dilating an eye with suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Mydriatics can precipitate an acute rise in intraocular pressure by further blocking aqueous outflow; acute angle closure is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day referral.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What is the gold-standard method of measuring intraocular pressure, and on what principle does it work?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), performed at the slit-lamp. It uses the Imbert-Fick principle: the force required to flatten a fixed 3.06 mm diameter of cornea is proportional to the IOP. It requires topical anaesthetic and fluorescein viewed under the cobalt blue filter.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What is the normal range of intraocular pressure?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Approximately 10-21 mmHg, with a mean of around 15-16 mmHg. There is mild diurnal variation, with pressures typically higher in the morning. IOP >21 mmHg with a normal disc and fields is termed ocular hypertension.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: How does central corneal thickness (CCT) affect Goldmann tonometry readings?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: GAT is calibrated to a CCT of about 520 micrometres. A thin cornea causes underestimation of the true IOP, while a thick cornea causes overestimation. IOP must therefore be interpreted alongside CCT, especially after refractive surgery like LASIK which thins the cornea.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: At the correct Goldmann end-point, what do you see and how do you calculate IOP?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Two fluorescein-stained semicircular mires appear under the cobalt blue filter. The dial is turned until the inner edges of the two semicircles just touch (S-shape). The dial reading is then multiplied by 10 to give the IOP in mmHg.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What clinical picture indicates acute angle-closure glaucoma, and what IOP is typical?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: A red, painful eye with a hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil, haloes around lights and reduced vision, often with nausea. IOP is typically very high (>40-50 mmHg). It is a sight-threatening emergency requiring same-day ophthalmology referral, and the eye must not be pharmacologically dilated.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why can't the iridocorneal angle be seen directly at the slit-lamp without a goniolens?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Light reflected from the angle recess exceeds the critical angle at the cornea-air interface and undergoes total internal reflection, so it never reaches the examiner. A goniolens with coupling fluid removes this interface and reflects the angle image out via mirrors.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: List the angle structures from anterior (corneal) to posterior (deepest).
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Schwalbe's line → trabecular meshwork → scleral spur → ciliary body band. Mnemonic: 'A Sad Trabecular Sees Ciliary'.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What is the quick rule distinguishing an open from an occludable angle?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: If the scleral spur is visible the angle is open; if the spur is hidden (only Schwalbe's line/anterior meshwork seen, or no structures) the angle is narrow/occludable or closed.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What does indentation (dynamic) gonioscopy add, and which lens is used?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Pressing on the cornea with a small-footplate four-mirror lens (Zeiss/Sussman) forces aqueous into the angle, distinguishing reversible appositional closure from permanent synechial closure caused by peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: How do Shaffer grades map to clinical risk?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Grade 4 (ciliary band, ~35-45°) and grade 3 (scleral spur, ~20-35°) are open with no closure risk; grade 2 (~20°) closure possible; grade 1 (~10°) closure probable; grade 0 (no structures) is a closed angle.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: In the swinging-light test, what defines a positive RAPD?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: The affected pupil paradoxically DILATES (rather than constricts) as the light swings onto it, because reduced afferent input on that side lowers total constrictor drive to both pupils.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Which cranial nerve/pathway does the swinging-light test assess?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex: retina and optic nerve (CN II). It does not test the efferent (CN III/parasympathetic) limb.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why do cataract and refractive error NOT cause a RAPD?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: They are media opacities that scatter or blur light but do not reduce optic nerve conduction, so afferent signalling remains intact and symmetric. A RAPD reflects true retinal or optic nerve dysfunction.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: List classic causes of a RAPD.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Optic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, central retinal artery occlusion, large retinal detachment, and dense asymmetric glaucoma.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why is the RAPD called a 'relative' defect?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: It compares the two eyes and only manifests when there is asymmetry between them. Bilateral symmetric optic neuropathy produces no RAPD despite reduced vision in both eyes.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What does fluorescein stain and under what light is it viewed?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: It pools in and binds areas of epithelial loss (bare stroma) and fluoresces bright green under cobalt-blue light. An intact lipid-rich epithelium does not take up the dye.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What fluorescein pattern is characteristic of herpes simplex keratitis?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: A branching (dendritic) linear ulcer with terminal end-bulbs. A broad 'map-like' amoeboid defect is a geographic ulcer, seen in advanced or steroid-modified HSV.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What is the Seidel test and a positive result?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Concentrated fluorescein is applied over a suspected corneal wound; a positive test shows a bright stream of aqueous diluting the dye into a dark rivulet, indicating a full-thickness leak/perforation (emergency).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: Why must corticosteroids not be given alone for a dendritic ulcer?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Topical steroids promote HSV viral replication and can convert a dendrite into a sight-threatening geographic ulcer. Treat with topical aciclovir; steroids only ever under specialist supervision.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: What does fine scattered punctate fluorescein staining suggest, and why remove contact lenses first?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Punctate epithelial erosions suggest dry eye, exposure or toxicity. Soft contact lenses absorb fluorescein and stain permanently, so they must be removed before the dye is instilled.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.front: How do you tell a surgical from a medical third-nerve palsy, and why does it matter?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Core Exam.back: Pupil-involving (fixed dilated) + painful CN III palsy = compressive (posterior communicating artery aneurysm) — peripheral parasympathetic fibres are hit early → urgent CT/MR angiography. Pupil-sparing CN III = microvascular (diabetes/hypertension).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What does a defect respecting the vertical midline localise to?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: The optic chiasm or a post-chiasmal lesion (tract, radiation, or occipital cortex). Monocular defects, by contrast, localise in front of the chiasm to the retina or optic nerve.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Classic field defect of chiasmal compression (e.g. pituitary adenoma)?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Bitemporal hemianopia — loss of both temporal fields due to compression of the crossing nasal retinal fibres at the chiasm.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Which field defects are characteristic of glaucoma?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Arcuate scotomata and nasal steps arising from retinal nerve fibre layer loss; these respect the horizontal midline and are detected on Humphrey static perimetry.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What causes macular sparing in a homonymous hemianopia and where is the lesion?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: An occipital (cortical) lesion; the macular representation at the occipital pole has a dual blood supply, so it is spared in occipital infarction.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Field defect from a temporal lobe lesion affecting Meyer's loop?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia — the classic 'pie in the sky' defect.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What physical principle underlies OCT imaging?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Low-coherence interferometry: near-infrared light is split into reference and sample beams, and back-scattered light from retinal layers is recombined so the interference pattern maps tissue reflectivity against depth, building cross-sectional B-scans at ~5-7 micrometre axial resolution.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What does intraretinal or subretinal fluid on macular OCT indicate?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Active exudative disease - wet (neovascular) AMD or diabetic macular oedema - and it is the key indication to start and to continue anti-VEGF therapy.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: How does OCT contribute to glaucoma care?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: It quantifies peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell layer thickness plus disc parameters (cup:disc ratio, rim area) against a normative database, detecting thinning for diagnosis and tracking progression over serial scans.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Why can high myopes get false 'red' RNFL results on OCT?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: The normative database assumes an average axial length; long myopic eyes and large or tilted discs fall outside those norms, producing false abnormal (red-disease) readings, while thick tissue can mask early loss (green-disease).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What are the practical advantages of OCT over fundus fluorescein angiography?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: OCT is quick, non-invasive, non-contact and dye-free (no risk of anaphylaxis), can be done through an undilated pupil, and gives quantitative cross-sectional structural detail - but it shows structure, not leakage or perfusion.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What does fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) image, and how?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: It images the retinal and choroidal circulation dynamically. Sodium fluorescein is injected intravenously and a rapid sequence of fundus photographs (blue excitation, yellow-green barrier filter) captures dye transit through arterial, arteriovenous, venous and late phases, revealing perfusion, leakage, ischaemia and neovascularisation.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Distinguish hyperfluorescence from hypofluorescence on FFA and their causes.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Hyperfluorescence (too bright) = leakage, window defect (RPE atrophy exposing choroid), staining, or neovascular vessels. Hypofluorescence (too dark) = blockage by overlying haemorrhage/exudate/pigment, or non-perfusion/filling defect from capillary dropout or arterial occlusion.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: List the normal phases of an FFA in order after injection.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Choroidal flush (~10 s), arterial phase (~10-15 s), arteriovenous/laminar venous phase (~15-20 s), venous phase (~20-30 s), and late phase (~5-10 min) when only abnormal leakage or staining remains bright.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What are the main adverse effects and safety requirements of FFA?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Transient yellow skin and urine (24-48 h), nausea/vomiting, vasovagal reactions and painful extravasation; rarely urticaria, bronchospasm and anaphylaxis. Resuscitation facilities and trained staff must be immediately available; use caution in renal impairment and generally avoid in pregnancy.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: How does a window defect differ from leakage on FFA, and why does it matter?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A window defect is bright early and fades as dye washes out (RPE atrophy letting choroidal fluorescence through, e.g. dry AMD). Leakage starts faint and grows progressively brighter and more blurred with time (active CNV or macular oedema). Only leakage indicates treatable wet disease.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What is the Amsler grid used to detect, and at what distance / correction is it tested?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A hand-held grid of straight lines with a central dot to detect central (macular) dysfunction. Tested one eye at a time, wearing reading glasses, held at ~30 cm in good light, fixating the central dot.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What does metamorphopsia on the Amsler grid mean and localise to?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Metamorphopsia = wavy, bent or distorted lines, caused by displacement/swelling of macular photoreceptors (subretinal fluid or oedema). It localises pathology to the macula, not the optic nerve or ocular media.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Why is the Amsler grid given to patients with dry AMD for home use?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: For weekly home monitoring so that new distortion or a central scotoma is caught early, flagging possible conversion to wet AMD, which prompts urgent OCT and review while anti-VEGF therapy can still preserve vision.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Give three limitations of the Amsler grid.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: It is subjective and fixation-dependent; the brain can perceptually fill in scotomas so small defects are missed (a normal grid does not exclude disease); and it requires reading correction, with cataract/refractive error confounding results. It monitors but does not diagnose.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Besides AMD, name conditions the Amsler grid can reveal.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Macular oedema (diabetic maculopathy, retinal vein occlusion, post-operative cystoid macular oedema), macular hole, epiretinal membrane (macular pucker), and as an adjunct in hydroxychloroquine maculopathy screening.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What is the main indication for B-scan ocular ultrasound?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: To image the posterior segment when the fundal view is obscured by opaque media (dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage, hyphaema), and to characterise intraocular/orbital masses. It is quick, bedside, and involves no ionising radiation.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: How is a retinal detachment distinguished from a posterior vitreous detachment on B-scan?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A retinal detachment is a thicker, brighter membrane tethered to the optic disc (funnel/V-shaped) with limited after-movement. A PVD is a thin, highly mobile membrane that is NOT attached at the disc and shows marked after-movement on dynamic scanning.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What is the 'T-sign' on B-scan and what does it indicate?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A right-angled anechoic fluid collection where fluid in Tenon's space meets the optic nerve shadow, with scleral thickening. It is the classic sign of posterior scleritis.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What are the classic B-scan features of a choroidal melanoma?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A dome- or collar-stud (mushroom) shaped solid mass with low internal reflectivity, acoustic hollowing/quiet zone, and sometimes choroidal excavation. Retinoblastoma differs by showing high reflectivity with calcification and acoustic shadowing.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What is the key safety contraindication to B-scan ocular ultrasound?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: A suspected open (ruptured) globe or penetrating injury. Probe pressure on the eye can express intraocular contents and cause irreversible sight loss; shield the eye and obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment and CT instead.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Who is invited to UK diabetic eye screening and how often?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Everyone with type 1 or type 2 diabetes aged 12 and over, invited for annual dilated two-field digital retinal photography of each eye.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: What do the R0–R3 grades mean?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: R0 = no retinopathy, R1 = background, R2 = pre-proliferative, R3 = proliferative (new vessels).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Which screening grades are referred to the hospital eye service?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: R2 (pre-proliferative), R3 (proliferative) and M1 (maculopathy). R1/M0 remain in routine annual recall.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Which drop is used to dilate pupils for screening and what is a key caveat?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Tropicamide 1% (short-acting mydriatic). It blurs near vision, precludes driving for hours, and should be avoided if acute angle-closure glaucoma is suspected.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: Why does diabetic retinopathy screening matter clinically?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults — and the commonest preventable one — and is asymptomatic early; screening enables timely laser (PRP) or anti-VEGF before vision is lost.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.front: A new bitemporal hemianopia is found — what are the next steps?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Imaging &.back: Chiasmal compression, usually a pituitary adenoma: arrange urgent MRI pituitary/brain AND a pituitary hormone profile (prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol/ACTH, TFTs, LH/FSH), with endocrinology and neurosurgery referral.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Define papilloedema and what distinguishes it from other causes of disc swelling.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Papilloedema is BILATERAL optic disc swelling caused specifically by raised intracranial pressure. Disc swelling from other causes (e.g. optic neuritis, ischaemia) is termed disc oedema, not papilloedema.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: List the classic fundoscopic features of papilloedema.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Blurred/elevated disc margins, loss of the physiological cup, obscured vessels crossing the disc margin, a hyperaemic disc, and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation. Acute cases show Paton's lines, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What happens to visual acuity and the blind spot in early papilloedema?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Visual acuity is characteristically preserved early, and the blind spot is enlarged on perimetry. Acuity loss and peripheral field constriction are late features of chronic or severe disease.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Name four important causes of papilloedema.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Space-occupying lesion (tumour/abscess/haemorrhage), idiopathic intracranial hypertension, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and malignant hypertension.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Why must a lumbar puncture never precede imaging in suspected papilloedema?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Papilloedema indicates raised ICP; if a space-occupying lesion is present, LP can precipitate fatal cerebral (tonsillar) herniation ('coning'). Urgent neuroimaging (CT/MRI with venography) must exclude a mass first.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What causes the pallor seen in optic atrophy?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Loss of retinal ganglion cell axons leads to regression of the superficial capillary network on the disc, so the underlying white lamina cribrosa and glial tissue show through, replacing the normal pink hue.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: List the four key associated findings of optic atrophy.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Reduced visual acuity, dyschromatopsia (red desaturation), a visual field defect, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) when damage is unilateral or asymmetric.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: How do you distinguish glaucomatous from non-glaucomatous optic disc changes?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Glaucoma causes pathological CUPPING first (cup:disc >= 0.6, thinned rim, raised IOP). Non-glaucomatous causes produce PALLOR with a normal-sized cup. Pallor out of proportion to cupping points to a neurological cause.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Why can a pink, normal-looking disc not exclude serious optic nerve disease?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Pallor is a late sign, taking about 4-6 weeks to develop after an acute insult. An acutely damaged nerve (e.g. recent optic neuritis) may look normal or even swollen before it later turns pale.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Name the six broad cause categories of optic atrophy.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Vascular (ischaemic optic neuropathy), inflammatory (optic neuritis/MS), compressive (tumour), glaucomatous (chronic glaucoma), toxic/nutritional (B12, methanol, ethambutol), and hereditary (Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What is a Roth spot?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: A retinal haemorrhage with a pale/white centre, seen on fundoscopy. The white core is composed of fibrin, platelet aggregate, or clustered inflammatory/white cells surrounded by a rim of haemorrhage.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Which infective condition is classically associated with Roth spots?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Infective endocarditis. However Roth spots are non-specific, so the finding should trigger blood cultures and echocardiography only when the clinical picture (fever, murmur) fits.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: List the non-endocarditis causes of Roth spots.
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Leukaemia, severe anaemia (often with thrombocytopenia), diabetes, hypertension, and hypoxia/high-altitude retinopathy (also HIV and connective-tissue disease).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What first-line investigations follow a Roth spot when leukaemia versus endocarditis is suspected?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Leukaemia: FBC with blood film then haematology referral. Endocarditis: three sets of blood cultures plus echocardiography (transthoracic then transoesophageal).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Why is a Roth spot described as 'a clue, not a diagnosis'?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: It is a shared final pathway of retinal microvascular injury common to many systemic diseases, so it confirms none of them alone; its value is prompting a directed search for the underlying cause.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What are Kayser-Fleischer rings and what causes them?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Golden-brown to greenish rings at the corneal periphery (limbus) caused by copper deposition in Descemet's membrane. They are the classic slit-lamp sign of Wilson's disease.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Which examination is required to reliably detect KF rings, especially early ones?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy; faint early rings may be visible only on gonioscopy. Bedside/torch inspection is unreliable.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What is the underlying metabolic defect in Wilson's disease?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Mutations in the ATP7B copper-transporting ATPase impair biliary copper excretion and caeruloplasmin loading, causing copper accumulation in liver, brain, kidneys and eye.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Which biochemical results support Wilson's disease alongside KF rings?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Low serum caeruloplasmin and raised 24-hour urinary copper excretion.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Does absence of KF rings exclude Wilson's disease?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: No. Rings are near-universal in neurological Wilson's but may be absent in early or purely hepatic disease, especially in children.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What is instilled in the phenylephrine blanching test and at what concentration?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Topical phenylephrine 2.5% (an alpha-agonist vasoconstrictor). The lower 2.5% strength is used rather than 10% to avoid systemic hypertensive effects.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: Which vessels blanch with phenylephrine and which do not?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: The superficial episcleral vascular plexus constricts and blanches (episcleritis). The deep scleral vessels do not constrict, so redness persists (scleritis).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: How do you interpret blanching versus no blanching?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Blanching (redness fades) = superficial injection = episcleritis, which is benign and self-limiting. No blanching = deep injection = scleritis, a painful, sight-threatening emergency.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What clinical features accompany scleritis and distinguish it from episcleritis?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Scleritis causes severe boring pain (worse at night, may wake the patient), globe tenderness on palpation, and a bluish/violaceous scleral hue. Episcleritis is non-tender with only mild irritation.

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: What systemic associations and treatment does scleritis require?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: Scleritis is associated with systemic vasculitis such as rheumatoid arthritis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis. It needs urgent ophthalmology referral and systemic anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive therapy (NSAIDs, systemic steroids, or steroid-sparing agents).

investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.front: How does a pale unilateral swollen disc differ from papilloedema, and what is the emergency action?
investigations__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Fundoscop.back: A pale, unilateral swollen disc suggests anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy; papilloedema is hyperaemic and bilateral (raised ICP). If arteritic (giant cell arteritis): check ESR/CRP + platelets and give high-dose steroids immediately — do NOT delay for temporal artery biopsy — to save the fellow eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 4-year-old has an eye that turns inwards. Testing shows reduced vision in that eye, but the eye is structurally normal on examination. What is the term for the reduced vision?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Reduced vision from abnormal visual development in a structurally normal eye is amblyopia; the misalignment itself is strabismus, one of its commonest causes. Anisometropia is a difference in refractive error between the eyes — a cause of amblyopia rather than the visual deficit itself. Nystagmus and diplopia are different phenomena: the deviating eye here is suppressed, which is precisely why the child does not see double.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: What is the most common type of squint seen in children?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Concomitant esotropia (a convergent squint with the same angle in all directions of gaze) is the commonest childhood squint, often accommodative.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A long-sighted (hypermetropic) 3-year-old has a convergent squint that disappears when wearing the prescribed glasses. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: The diagnostic feature is that the deviation disappears with the full hypermetropic correction: the child was converging because of the accommodative effort needed to focus, and removing that effort removes the squint. Infantile esotropia presents in the first months of life with a large angle and little refractive error, and does not resolve in glasses. A sixth nerve palsy gives an incomitant deviation worse on gaze to the affected side, and Duane retraction syndrome limits abduction with globe retraction on adduction — neither is altered by a lens. Sensory esotropia follows poor vision in one eye, which glasses alone would not correct.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: Which test uses the position of the corneal light reflex to detect a manifest squint?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: The Hirschberg (corneal light reflex) test: the reflex is central and symmetrical in aligned eyes and displaced in the deviating eye in a manifest squint.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: On the cover–uncover test, the uncovered eye moves to take up fixation. What does this indicate?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: If the uncovered eye has to move to pick up fixation, it was not fixing to begin with — a manifest deviation, present all the time, which is what tropia means. A phoria is latent and appears only when fusion is broken, so it is unmasked by the alternate cover test rather than by cover–uncover. Properly aligned eyes with normal fusion show no movement of either eye, convergence insufficiency shows up on near-point-of-convergence testing, and pseudostrabismus gives a cross-eyed appearance with a completely normal cover test.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 2-year-old is brought in with a squint the parents first noticed a month ago. On examination the right pupil shows a white reflex instead of a red one. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate ophthalmology referral, seen within hours
Urgent suspected-cancer referral, seen in 2 weeks
Routine ophthalmology referral within six weeks
Cycloplegic refraction and glasses in the first instance
Patch the better-seeing eye and review in a month
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Immediate ophthalmology referral, seen within hours
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: A new-onset squint together with loss of the red reflex is referred immediately — seen within hours — because it may mean retinoblastoma or raised intracranial pressure (NICE). The two-week suspected-cancer pathway is the right answer for an absent red reflex found on its own, for example at a routine check, so the discriminator is the combination of signs rather than the white reflex alone. A new squint with ataxia, vomiting or headache is likewise an immediate referral, to acute paediatrics. Refraction, glasses and occlusion treat the consequences of poor vision and are irrelevant until a sight- and life-threatening cause has been excluded.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 3-year-old has a constant outward turn of the right eye, present for several months, with the same angle in every direction of gaze. Acuity is 6/6 in the left eye but only hand movements in the right. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: Vision loss causing the squint, not caused by it
A right sixth nerve palsy limiting abduction
Prominent epicanthic folds mimicking a squint
A latent squint that has decompensated with fatigue
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Vision loss causing the squint, not caused by it
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: An eye seeing only hand movements has vision far worse than suppression alone would produce, so this is a sensory squint — the eye has drifted because it cannot see, and the underlying ocular disease must be found. The discriminating features are the severity of the acuity loss and the outward drift, since a young child's refractive squint is typically convergent and leaves useful vision in the deviating eye. Hypermetropic over-accommodation drives the eye inwards, and a sixth nerve palsy gives an incomitant convergent deviation worse on right gaze. This child needs the red reflex, dilated fundoscopy and urgent referral to exclude cataract, retinal disease and retinoblastoma.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 6-month-old is brought in because she looks cross-eyed in photographs. The corneal light reflex is symmetrical and central, the cover test is normal, and both red reflexes are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Infantile esotropia with a large angle
A left sixth nerve palsy with esotropia
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Prominent epicanthic folds or a broad nasal bridge cover the nasal sclera and make the eyes look convergent when they are correctly aligned — the appearance is real but the deviation is not. Two findings settle it: a symmetrical, central corneal light reflex, and a cover test in which neither eye moves to take up fixation. Infantile esotropia, accommodative esotropia and a sixth nerve palsy would all displace the light reflex in the deviating eye and produce a refixation movement, and the normal red reflexes exclude a deprivational cause. Reassure — but epicanthic folds can coexist with a true squint, so refer if there is any doubt about the cover test or the vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 5-year-old with strabismic amblyopia has worn his full glasses correction for four months, but acuity in the deviating eye remains reduced. Which treatment is used next?
options: Occlusion or atropine penalisation of the better eye
Occlusion or atropine penalisation of the worse eye
Extraocular muscle recession and resection surgery
Prism spectacles worn in front of the amblyopic eye only
Vision therapy exercises done with both eyes open
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Occlusion or atropine penalisation of the better eye
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Amblyopia is a cortical problem, so the weaker eye improves only when the brain is forced to use it — the better eye is therefore penalised, by patching or by atropine drops that blur its near vision. Penalising the worse eye is the classic error and would deepen the amblyopia. Surgery realigns the eyes but does nothing for the acuity of an amblyopic eye and is reserved for a deviation persisting after glasses and occlusion. Prisms shift an image without improving cortical development, and exercises with both eyes open let the good eye keep dominating — exactly what the treatment has to prevent.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 9-year-old is seen for the first time with long-standing left strabismic amblyopia that has never been treated. What is the most likely outcome for that eye?
options: Reduced acuity in that eye with poor stereopsis
Full recovery of acuity once glasses are worn full-time
Normal acuity but troublesome double vision
Progressive loss of vision in both eyes
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Reduced acuity in that eye with poor stereopsis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Amblyopia responds best while the visual system is plastic, so a child presenting near the end of that window is likely to keep reduced acuity in the affected eye and to lose binocular depth perception — this is the commonest cause of monocular visual impairment in children and young adults. Glasses correct the optics but cannot by themselves reverse established cortical suppression. Double vision does not occur because the deviating eye is suppressed, and the fellow eye is unaffected, so vision does not deteriorate bilaterally. Some further improvement is still worth attempting at this age, but it does not happen spontaneously.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: Amblyopia treatment depends on the visual system still being plastic. Within which window is it most effective?
options: Before about 7–8 years, while vision is still plastic
Only within the first three months of life
Between about 10 and 16 years, during adolescence
At any age, since adults respond as well as children
Only once the child is old enough to read a letter chart
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Before about 7–8 years, while vision is still plastic
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: Cortical visual development is plastic in early childhood, so occlusion or atropine penalisation gives the best acuity gains when started before about 7–8 years; response rates fall off after that and adults do not respond. The window opens at birth rather than closing at three months, and by adolescence the pathway is largely fixed. Waiting until the child can read a letter chart wastes the very years in which treatment works — preverbal acuity tests exist precisely so that treatment need not wait. Some benefit is still possible in older primary-school children, so a late presentation is treated rather than abandoned.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 6-week-old is found on the infant check to have a dense white cataract in one eye. If this is not treated promptly, which type of amblyopia is she at risk of?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: A dense unilateral cataract stops any formed image reaching the retina, so that eye's cortical pathway never develops — stimulus-deprivation amblyopia, the most severe type and the most urgent to treat. Strabismic and anisometropic amblyopia arise from a suppressed or blurred image rather than an absent one, and both need a squint or unequal refraction this baby does not have. Meridional and ametropic amblyopia follow uncorrected astigmatism and high bilateral error. The discriminator is total obstruction of the visual axis, which is why the cataract is removed early rather than corrected with glasses.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: An 8-year-old with previously straight eyes develops a squint whose angle varies with the direction of gaze, together with headaches that are worst on waking. What does this most likely indicate?
options: An incomitant squint from a neurological cause
A concomitant esotropia that needs glasses
A decompensating latent squint (phoria) causing headache
Pseudostrabismus from a broad nasal bridge
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: An incomitant squint from a neurological cause
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: A squint whose angle changes with gaze direction is incomitant, meaning a paralytic or restrictive cause rather than the benign refractive squints of early childhood — with new onset in an older child and early-morning headache this points to a cranial nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure or a tumour, and warrants urgent neuroimaging. A decompensating phoria is the trap: it does cause headache and eye strain, but the angle stays the same in all directions of gaze. Accommodative and intermittent squints are concomitant and do not cause morning headache, and pseudostrabismus produces no true deviation on cover testing.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 4-year-old has fully accommodative esotropia with amblyopia in the deviating eye. The eyes are structurally normal with clear media and normal red reflexes. What is the correct order of management?
options: Glasses first, then amblyopia therapy, then surgery if needed
Amblyopia therapy first, then glasses, then surgery if needed
Surgery first, then glasses, then amblyopia therapy afterwards
Glasses first, then surgery, with no amblyopia therapy needed
Surgery alone, since glasses do not affect the angle of squint
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Glasses first, then amblyopia therapy, then surgery if needed
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: In accommodative esotropia the hypermetropia is the cause, so the full cycloplegic correction is given first and often straightens the eyes on its own; patching or atropine penalisation of the better eye then follows for any residual amblyopia. Patching before the refraction is corrected forces the weaker eye to work through an uncorrected blur. Surgery is reserved for a deviation that persists after glasses and amblyopia treatment. Note the exceptions to this sequence: deprivation such as a congenital cataract is removed first and urgently, and in infantile esotropia surgery is the primary treatment, done early.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: A 5-year-old has straight eyes on cover testing, full eye movements and normal red reflexes. Cycloplegic refraction is +0.50 in the right eye and +5.00 in the left. With the full correction worn, acuity is 6/6 right and 6/24 left. What is the most likely cause of the reduced vision?
options: Anisometropic amblyopia in the left eye
Strabismic amblyopia from a latent squint
A left optic nerve or retinal disorder
Uncorrected refractive error alone, not amblyopia
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Anisometropic amblyopia in the left eye
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: A large difference in refractive error between the eyes leaves one retinal image chronically blurred, so that eye is suppressed and fails to develop — anisometropic amblyopia, easily missed because the eyes look straight and the child has no symptoms. The discriminating feature is that acuity stays at 6/24 with the full correction in place, which excludes simple uncorrected refractive error and is what defines amblyopia. Strabismic amblyopia needs a manifest deviation, which the cover test excludes, and stimulus deprivation needs a media opacity, which the normal red reflex excludes. A structural cause is unlikely here, but fundoscopy should still confirm it before labelling the eye amblyopic.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.question: In a 3-year-old with a convergent squint, refraction is performed after cyclopentolate drops rather than without them. Why?
options: Accommodation would otherwise hide the full hypermetropia
It relaxes the extraocular muscles so the angle can be measured
It anaesthetises the cornea so the reading is comfortable
It dilates the pupil so that visual acuity can be tested
It stops the child blinking during the measurement
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.answer: Accommodation would otherwise hide the full hypermetropia
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Strabismus (S.explanation: A young child's ciliary muscle is powerful enough to accommodate through much of a hypermetropic error, so an uncycloplegic refraction systematically under-reads it — and it is precisely that hidden long-sightedness that drives the over-accommodation causing the esotropia. Paralysing accommodation reveals the full correction that must be prescribed if the glasses are to straighten the eyes. Cycloplegics act on the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter, not the extraocular muscles, so the angle of squint is measured separately by prism cover test. They are not anaesthetics, and although the pupil dilates as a side effect, that is for fundus examination.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A 24-year-old with deranged liver function, a tremor and personality change is noted to have a brownish-green ring at the edge of the cornea. What is this sign and its cause?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: A Kayser–Fleischer ring is copper deposited in Descemet's membrane at the corneal periphery — a brownish-green rim, densest above and below — and with liver derangement, tremor and personality change in a young adult it means Wilson's disease. Corneal arcus is a white-grey ring separated from the limbus by a clear zone and, under 45, points to familial hypercholesterolaemia rather than copper. Band keratopathy is chalky-white calcium in a horizontal interpalpebral band, and corneal verticillata is a fine whorl in the epithelium from amiodarone — neither is a limbal ring.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient with fever and a new heart murmur has retinal haemorrhages with pale centres on fundoscopy. What are these?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with a pale or white centre of fibrin and inflammatory cells, which is why they signal an embolic or haematological process — infective endocarditis, leukaemia, severe anaemia and hyperviscosity. Cotton-wool spots are nerve fibre layer infarcts with fluffy edges and no haemorrhage, and hard exudates are yellow lipid deposits with sharp margins. Dot-and-blot haemorrhages lie deep in the retina and are uniformly dark, with no pale centre.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A tall patient with arachnodactyly and aortic root dilatation is found to have a dislocated lens. In which direction does the lens typically displace?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: In Marfan syndrome the zonular fibres are stretched but intact, so the lens rides up and out. In homocystinuria the zonules disintegrate, so the lens drops down and in and may fall forward into the anterior chamber and cause pupil-block glaucoma — an emergency that does not happen in Marfan. Complete posterior dislocation into the vitreous follows trauma or total zonular loss rather than either inherited condition.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A young man with a marfanoid habitus, learning difficulty and a history of venous thromboembolism has a downward lens dislocation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Homocystinuria is autosomal recessive: a marfanoid build plus learning difficulty, osteoporosis and a strong venous and arterial thrombotic tendency, with the lens displaced down and in. Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, with normal intellect, no thrombophilia and upward displacement — the systemic features, not the lens alone, separate them. Weill–Marchesani patients are short with brachydactyly and a small spherical lens, and Stickler syndrome causes high myopia and retinal detachment rather than ectopia lentis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A young man with ankylosing spondylitis develops a recurrent, unilateral, painful red eye with photophobia. What is the most likely ocular diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: A recurrent, unilateral, painful and photophobic red eye with circumcorneal injection, cells and flare and a small or irregular pupil is acute anterior uveitis — the classic HLA-B27 association shared by ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, IBD and psoriatic arthritis. Conjunctivitis is sticky, usually bilateral, and neither painful nor photophobic; episcleritis and scleritis redden the sclera without anterior chamber cells. Acute angle-closure glaucoma gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil, a hazy cornea, a stony-hard globe and vomiting.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis has a deep, boring, painful red eye with a bluish hue and tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Scleritis gives deep, boring, night-waking pain with globe tenderness and a violaceous hue best seen in daylight; the bedside discriminator is that the deep vessels do not blanch with topical phenylephrine, whereas episcleritis blanches and is uncomfortable rather than painful. Anterior uveitis causes photophobia with circumcorneal injection, cells and flare and a small or irregular pupil, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis produces a crescentic corneal infiltrate with thinning at the limbus. In rheumatoid arthritis scleritis is the sight-threatening one and needs systemic immunosuppression, not topical treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 30 has 'pizza-pie' retinal haemorrhages and exudate. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: CMV retinitis occurs once the CD4 count falls below about 50 and is a full-thickness necrotising retinitis, giving the 'pizza-pie' mix of dense haemorrhage and yellow-white exudate spreading along the vascular arcades. HIV retinopathy is scattered cotton-wool spots with minimal haemorrhage and does not threaten vision. Toxoplasma chorioretinitis is a focal 'headlight in the fog' lesion with vitritis, usually next to an old pigmented scar, and a central retinal vein occlusion causes sudden painless loss with a swollen disc and haemorrhages in all four quadrants.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: Both pupils are small and irregular. They constrict briskly when the patient focuses on a near target but do not react to a bright light, and they dilate poorly with mydriatic drops. Deep tendon reflexes are normal. What is this sign and its classic cause?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Argyll Robertson and Holmes–Adie pupils both show light-near dissociation, so the pupil itself has to be described. Argyll Robertson pupils are small, irregular and bilateral, constrict briskly to near and dilate poorly — neurosyphilis. A Holmes–Adie pupil is large, unilateral and round, constricts slowly and tonically with slow redilation, typically in a young woman with absent reflexes. A Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD) is normal in size and dilates when the light swings from the good eye to the affected eye, and Horner's is a small pupil with partial ptosis but an intact light reaction.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A 72-year-old has sudden painless loss of vision in one eye, with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and an ESR of 90. What is the most important immediate management?
options: Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment
Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: This is giant cell arteritis causing arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and the fellow eye can be lost within days, so steroids come before any investigation — intravenous methylprednisolone where vision is already affected. Temporal artery biopsy and/or ultrasound is arranged afterwards and still shows arteritic change for a week or two after steroids start; waiting for it is the classic error. Ocular massage and anterior chamber paracentesis are manoeuvres for non-arteritic central retinal artery occlusion, and anti-VEGF treats neovascular macular disease.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A 9-year-old with multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling is found on slit-lamp examination to have several small tan, dome-shaped raised lesions on both irides. What are these and what is the diagnosis?
options: Iris freckles — a common benign variant
Iris melanoma — a pigmented iris tumour
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Lisch nodules are melanocytic iris hamartomas — raised, dome-shaped and tan — present in almost all adults with neurofibromatosis type 1, alongside café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling and the risk of optic nerve glioma. Brushfield spots are flat speckled white-grey rings in the peripheral iris of Down syndrome and iris freckles are flat pigmented patches, so the discriminator is that Lisch nodules are raised. Koeppe nodules sit at the pupil margin in granulomatous uveitis with a red photophobic eye, and an iris melanoma is a solitary enlarging mass rather than multiple bilateral lesions.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient reports drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse in the evening and after prolonged reading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Fatigability is the whole diagnosis: ptosis and diplopia that worsen with sustained upgaze or towards the end of the day, with normal pupils, indicate myasthenia gravis, and ocular signs are the first presentation in most patients. A third nerve palsy is fixed rather than fatigable, with complete ptosis, a 'down and out' eye and often a dilated pupil; Horner's gives partial ptosis with a small pupil and no diplopia. Thyroid eye disease causes lid retraction rather than ptosis with constant restrictive diplopia, and an internuclear ophthalmoplegia gives failure of adduction with nystagmus in the abducting eye.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: Which drug requires regular retinal monitoring because it can cause a bull's-eye maculopathy?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in the retinal pigment epithelium and can cause an irreversible bull's-eye maculopathy, so monitoring with OCT and autofluorescence runs annually once treatment passes five years — earlier in higher-risk patients, and with no routine baseline test in the UK (RCOphth). Ethambutol also needs visual checks, but its toxicity is a dose-related optic neuropathy affecting acuity and colour vision, not a maculopathy. Amiodarone causes corneal verticillata, vigabatrin irreversible peripheral field constriction, and topiramate bilateral acute angle-closure with a myopic shift.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient on long-term anti-tuberculous therapy develops reduced visual acuity and impaired colour vision. Which drug is the most likely cause?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Ethambutol causes a dose-related toxic optic neuropathy that affects red–green colour vision and central acuity before anything is visible at the disc, so acuity and colour vision are checked before starting and the drug is stopped at the first sign of change. Isoniazid's characteristic toxicity is a pyridoxine-responsive peripheral neuropathy — isoniazid optic neuropathy exists but is rare. Rifampicin colours secretions orange and stains soft lenses, pyrazinamide causes hepatitis and gout, and streptomycin damages the vestibulocochlear nerve rather than the optic nerve.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient has bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, lid lag and diplopia on upgaze. Which underlying systemic condition is most likely?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Lid retraction with lid lag is essentially specific to thyroid eye disease and is what separates Graves' orbitopathy from other causes of proptosis; the diplopia comes from a restrictive myopathy of the inferior and medial recti, not a nerve palsy. Orbital lymphoma and sarcoid infiltration push the eye forward without retracting the lid, and a carotid–cavernous fistula gives pulsatile proptosis with chemosis, dilated conjunctival vessels and an orbital bruit. Most patients are hyperthyroid, but thyroid eye disease also occurs in euthyroid and hypothyroid patients, and the sight-threat is compressive optic neuropathy rather than the proptosis itself.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A 28-year-old with a raised BMI reports daily headaches and brief episodes of greying-out of vision. Blood pressure is 128/78. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Papilloedema means disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure, and transient visual obscurations with preserved acuity and an enlarged blind spot are its hallmark; a false-localising sixth nerve palsy may accompany it. Optic neuritis is usually unilateral, painful on eye movement and causes early loss of acuity and colour vision with an RAPD, and the disc is often normal because the lesion is retrobulbar. Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is unilateral, sudden and altitudinal, and accelerated hypertension would show a markedly raised blood pressure with flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.question: A patient has unilateral ptosis, a constricted pupil and reduced sweating on the same side of the face. What is the syndrome?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Systemic Dise.explanation: Ptosis with miosis and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis is Horner's syndrome, an interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway; the ptosis is partial because only Müller's muscle is denervated, the pupil is small but still reacts to light, and the anisocoria is greater in dim light. A third nerve palsy is the opposite — complete ptosis with a large unreactive pupil and a down-and-out eye. Holmes–Adie gives a large tonic pupil with no ptosis, and myasthenic ptosis is fatigable with entirely normal pupils.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A 25-year-old develops red, watery eyes over 3 days — the second eye starting after the first — following a head cold. There is a tender preauricular lymph node and follicles on the everted lower lid; vision is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: A preceding upper respiratory infection, watery discharge, second-eye involvement a few days after the first, follicles on the everted lid and a tender preauricular node are classic for adenoviral conjunctivitis. Vision is normal, which argues against uveitis and angle-closure.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: Which single finding most reliably points to a VIRAL rather than a bacterial or allergic conjunctivitis?
options: Redness that becomes bilateral within days
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: A tender preauricular node is characteristic of viral conjunctivitis (it is also found in chlamydial and gonococcal infection) and is typically absent in bacterial and allergic disease. Watery discharge occurs in allergic conjunctivitis too, and bilateral redness, mild photophobia and lid swelling occur in all three.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: On everting the eyelid of a patient with suspected viral conjunctivitis, which conjunctival reaction would you expect?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis produces follicles — pale, dome-shaped lymphoid aggregates, most numerous in the lower fornix. They are also seen in chlamydial disease. Papillae (each with a central vessel) point to bacterial or allergic causes; giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsus suggest vernal disease, as do limbal Horner-Trantas dots.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A patient has a red eye with thick purulent discharge and lids stuck together on waking. Which type of conjunctivitis is most likely?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Thick purulent discharge with the lids glued together on waking is typical of bacterial conjunctivitis. Viral discharge is watery and allergic discharge is stringy and mucoid with prominent itch. Most bacterial conjunctivitis is still self-limiting and settles without antibiotics.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: What is the most common causative organism of viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Adenovirus causes the great majority of viral conjunctivitis, and in adults it is the commonest cause of infective conjunctivitis overall. In young children the balance shifts — bacterial causes predominate in that age group.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: During a local outbreak, a patient has a severe, highly contagious conjunctivitis with photophobia, blurred vision and subepithelial corneal infiltrates. What is the diagnosis?
options: Pharyngoconjunctival fever with a sore throat
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is the most severe adenoviral form and spreads readily through households and eye clinics. Subepithelial corneal infiltrates appear as the conjunctivitis settles and can cause glare and blurred vision for weeks to months; pseudomembranes may form. Management is supportive, with steroids only under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A child presents with fever, a sore throat and bilateral follicular conjunctivitis. Which adenoviral syndrome is this?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Fever, pharyngitis and bilateral follicular conjunctivitis together make up pharyngoconjunctival fever, an adenoviral syndrome of children that often spreads through schools and swimming pools. It is self-limiting and needs supportive care only.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: Aside from safety-netting, what is the single most important management action in viral conjunctivitis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Adenoviral conjunctivitis is highly contagious, so hygiene is the key intervention: thorough hand washing, a separate towel and flannel, not rubbing the eyes, not sharing pillows or eye make-up, and no contact lenses until the eye has been white for 24 hours. Routine exclusion from school, nursery or work is not required (UKHSA).

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: What is the first-line treatment for uncomplicated viral conjunctivitis?
options: A one-week course of topical chloramphenicol drops
Supportive care: lubricants and cool compresses
Topical corticosteroid drops, tapered over a month
Topical aciclovir ointment five times daily
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.answer: Supportive care: lubricants and cool compresses
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis is self-limiting, so treatment is supportive — artificial tears, cool compresses and simple analgesia, plus hygiene advice. Antibiotics do nothing for a viral infection, aciclovir treats herpes simplex rather than adenovirus, and steroids are not started in primary care.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: Why should topical steroids not be started empirically on an undifferentiated red eye?
options: They reliably cause cataract within a few days of starting
They can worsen an unrecognised herpetic dendritic ulcer
They clear the infection so fast that the diagnosis is missed
They enlarge the preauricular node and confuse the picture
They frequently cause an allergic reaction to the preservative
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.answer: They can worsen an unrecognised herpetic dendritic ulcer
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: If the red eye is actually herpes simplex, a topical steroid lets a dendritic ulcer enlarge into a geographic ulcer, with scarring and lasting visual loss. Prolonged steroid use also raises intraocular pressure and causes cataract, but the immediate danger is the missed dendritic ulcer — so steroids in conjunctivitis are started only under ophthalmology.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A soft contact-lens wearer presents with a painful red eye and blurred vision. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure and manage as a self-limiting viral conjunctivitis
Prescribe topical steroid drops and review in one week
Same-day ophthalmology referral for microbial keratitis
Prescribe oral antihistamines and lubricant eye drops
Advise cool compresses and chloramphenicol over the counter
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.answer: Same-day ophthalmology referral for microbial keratitis
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: A contact-lens wearer with a painful red eye and blurred vision has microbial keratitis until proven otherwise, including Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba. Stop lens wear, ask the patient to bring the lenses and case for culture, and refer the same day — do not treat as conjunctivitis.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A patient has a unilateral red eye with vesicles on the lid and a branching (dendritic) ulcer that stains with fluorescein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Adenoviral conjunctivitis with a corneal abrasion
Severe allergic conjunctivitis with punctate staining
Episcleritis with a sectoral patch of redness
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: A unilateral red eye with vesicles on the lid and a branching, fluorescein-staining dendritic ulcer indicates herpes simplex. Do not give topical steroids; refer the same day for a topical antiviral under ophthalmology supervision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A 3-day-old neonate has a purulent conjunctivitis. Which infection must be urgently excluded?
options: Adenoviral conjunctivitis caught from a sibling
Molluscum contagiosum of the lid margin
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Purulent conjunctivitis in the first days of life is ophthalmia neonatorum. Gonococcal infection is the emergency — it can perforate the cornea within a day or two — and chlamydial infection typically appears a little later and signals maternal infection. Both need same-day assessment, urgent swabs and systemic treatment.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: Which feature in a red eye should prompt same-day ophthalmology referral rather than a diagnosis of simple conjunctivitis?
options: Redness spreading to the second eye
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Reduced acuity — along with severe pain, marked photophobia, ciliary flush, fluorescein staining of the cornea or contact-lens wear — points to keratitis, uveitis or angle-closure rather than conjunctivitis. Never reassure a red eye with reduced vision.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: A parent asks whether their child with viral conjunctivitis must stay off school. What is the correct UK advice?
options: No routine exclusion — reinforce hand hygiene and separate towels
Exclude from school until the eye is no longer red or discharging
Exclude until 48 hours of topical antibiotics are completed
Exclude for two weeks, as adenovirus is shed for that long
Exclude until a conjunctival swab confirms clearance
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.answer: No routine exclusion — reinforce hand hygiene and separate towels
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Conjunctivitis — viral or bacterial — does not routinely require exclusion from school or nursery, and a child who is otherwise well can attend (UKHSA). The control measure is hygiene: hand washing, a separate towel and flannel, and not rubbing or sharing eye contact. Health-protection advice is sought only if there is a cluster or outbreak.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.question: What is the usual natural history of uncomplicated viral conjunctivitis?
options: Chronic, lasting many months without treatment
Rapidly progressive and permanent vision loss
Requires long-term antibiotic drops to clear
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Viral (Adenov.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis settles on its own, typically over 1–3 weeks. Warn the patient that it characteristically gets worse before it gets better, peaking around days 3–5, and that the second eye often follows the first — otherwise they return convinced the treatment has failed. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis takes longer.

conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.question: A 29-year-old woman has 3 days of blurred vision in her left eye with pain on moving the eye and 'washed-out' colours. Acuity is reduced, colour vision is impaired, there is a left RAPD and the optic disc looks normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OPHTHALMOLOGY__Optic Neuriti.explanation: Subacute unilateral loss over days with pain on eye movement, dyschromatopsia and a RAPD is classic optic neuritis; a normal disc means it is retrobulbar (~2/3 of cases).
